study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional spatial econometric study (multilevel negative binomial regression of 31,383 Census block groups across nine U.S. states)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes cross-sectional observational associations between municipal incorporation status, neighborhood poverty, and unserved water/wastewater land area across 31,383 Census block groups using multilevel negative binomial regression at a single cross-section without longitudinal panel tracking or a quasi-experimental intervention evaluation design (such as DiD, RDD, IV, or ITS). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, quantitative observational cross-sectional regressions without a quasi-experimental intervention structure map directly to the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.
selection_bias: Some concern. Nine eastern U.S. states were purposively included (limiting generalizability to western states; PDF p. 10). Within those states, community land area (>= 250 parcels/sq mi) was comprehensively captured (n = 31,383 block groups), but restricting ACS poverty data to estimates with CV <= 40% (PDF p. 14) can disproportionately exclude small or sparsely populated block groups, and minor utilities without locatable physical addresses were omitted (PDF pp. 12-13).
measurement_bias: Some concern. Block groups are ecologically assigned to a single incorporation category by plurality/majority land area (PDF pp. 10-11), data layers span mismatched years (2010 Census/2008-2012 ACS vs. 2018 building footprints vs. ~2021 utility/parcel data), and outcome measurement for non-Tier-1 systems relies on municipal boundaries as service proxies (Tier 2b, e.g., 28% of Mississippi POTWs), regression-predicted circular buffers (Tier 3), convex hulls of lines, and deterministic parcel imputations in Florida—creating risk of differential misclassification near municipal borders (PDF pp. 12-14).
confounding: Some concern (moderate-to-high residual confounding risk). Multivariable negative binomial GLMs adjust for high poverty, population density, percent rural population, and county- and state-level random intercepts (PDF pp. 9-10), but omit critical within-county block-group confounders—most notably racial/ethnic composition (despite extensive discussion of racialized municipal underbounding on PDF pp. 1, 11, 14), housing/subdivision age, and sub-county soil/topographic suitability.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable to longitudinal loss (cross-sectional spatial administrative design), though sample exclusions occur from dropping block groups with low-reliability ACS poverty estimates (CV > 40%), 429 CWS (3.7%) and ~6% of POTWs lacking physical coordinates, and imputing 27% missing drinking water and 7% missing sewer parcel records in Florida (PDF pp. 12-14).
reporting_bias: Some concern / No pre-analysis plan reported. No pre-registration or protocol is cited, though the authors transparently report multiple model specifications (with and without county/state random effects and high-poverty interaction terms) for both sewer and drinking water outcomes across main figures and Supplementary Tables 5-6 (PDF pp. 5-9).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong with spatial/temporal caveats. Municipal incorporation status is systematically constructed from 2010 Census TIGER/Line and Census of Governments functional/class codes combined with 240 m Microsoft building footprint rasters, and unincorporated settlements are classified into Island, Fringe (1.6 km extraterritorial jurisdiction proxy), and Outlying types alongside state statutory annexation summaries (PDF pp. 2-4, 10-11). Caveats include a uniform 1.6 km ETJ proxy rather than state-specific statutory distances, majority-area ecological assignment at the block-group level, and temporal mismatch between 2010 municipal boundaries and 2018 building footprints.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate (some concern). While the authors assembled an extensive multi-state spatial dataset covering 96% of active CWS (n = 10,948) and 94% of POTWs in eight states (n = 5,220) plus 9.09 million Florida residential parcels (PDF pp. 11-14), service area polygons measure territorial coverage rather than verified household connections, and substantial reliance on Tier 2b municipal boundary proxies, Tier 3 circular buffers, line convex hulls, and Florida missing-data assumptions introduces spatial measurement error.
where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 1-2); Results — Types of unincorporated communities, Summary statistics, Regression results (PDF pp. 2-8); Methods — Negative binomial regression, Data overview, Identifying and categorizing communities, Centralized infrastructure coverage, Approximated service areas, Florida sewer coverage, Demographic data (PDF pp. 9-14).

study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods empirical study combining a quantitative non-randomized longitudinal comparative analysis of official municipal water/sanitation indicators (2000-2010) and corporate/inflation series (2003-2012) with qualitative semi-structured interviews (n = 15) analyzed via content and discourse analysis
why_tool_chosen: The study collects, analyzes, and integrates both primary qualitative data (15 recorded semi-structured interviews analyzed via content and discourse analysis) and quantitative comparative observational data (paired Wilcoxon and independent Mann-Whitney U tests comparing 2000-2008/2010 municipal indicator changes between 64 COPASA and 256 municipal-operator localities, alongside corporate longitudinal series), fitting MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative non-randomized (3.1-3.5) module.
overall_rating: High methodological concern in quantitative component (strong qualitative and integration components, but overall quality bounded by unadjusted non-randomized quantitative comparisons per MMAT 2018 guidance)
selection_bias: High concern: The longitudinal municipal comparison (64 COPASA vs 256 municipal operators) excludes over half of Minas Gerais's municipalities, omitting all localities with joint COPASA/municipal service and all municipalities newly acquired by COPASA after the 2006 IPO. Qualitative recruitment of 15 informants used purposive documentary and snowball sampling without reporting non-response or detailed participant counts in text (Table 1 rendered as an image).
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Quantitative exposure measurement conflates pre-IPO (2000-2005) and post-IPO (2006-2008/2010) periods, PNSB survey protocols changed between 2000 and 2008 (affecting sewage comparability), and quantitative data on supply regularity, intermittence, and rationing were unavailable. Qualitative interviews were recorded and transcribed, though the semi-structured guide is not provided.
confounding: High concern: Quantitative comparisons rely exclusively on unadjusted bivariate non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney U tests) with zero statistical control for baseline coverage ceiling effects, municipality size, socioeconomic status, macroeconomic conditions, the 2009 creation of regulator ARSAE, or federal non-repayable grants prioritizing small municipal utilities (all acknowledged qualitatively by the authors as major confounders).
attrition: Can't tell / moderate concern: Official IBGE Census (2000, 2010) and PNSB (2000, 2008) datasets have broad municipal coverage, but exact missingness and numeric cells in embedded table images (Tables 1-12) cannot be verified from the PDF text layer, and restricting the longitudinal analysis to continuously single-operator municipalities reduced sample counts from 67/128 (COPASA) and 346/284 (municipal) to 64 and 256 respectively.
reporting_bias: Moderate / No pre-registration information: No pre-specified protocol or analysis plan is reported, and embedded raster tables/figures prevent inspection of exact test statistics in the extracted text stream; however, the authors transparently report null findings (e.g., non-significant differences at 95% confidence for bathrooms and sewage network connections) alongside significant differences.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: Accurately characterizes the institutional nature of COPASA's 2006 stock-market IPO (mixed-capital company remaining under majority state control while adopting capital-market governance and post-2009 ARSAE tariff regulation), reviewing state legislation, decrees, and corporate filings, though exact statute/decree citations are omitted and the 2000-2008/2010 quantitative window conflates six pre-IPO years with two-to-four post-IPO years.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Draws on standard official administrative and census metrics (IBGE Census 2000/2010 household network and bathroom indicators, PNSB 2000/2008 water treatment volumes, Central Bank INPC/IPCA inflation vs COPASA tariff readjustments, and utility customer complaint records), but sewage comparability across PNSB waves was limited by protocol changes and operational continuity/intermittence relied solely on qualitative perceptions.
where_found: Research aims and institutional background on PDF Pages 1-4 (pp. 249-252) and PDF Page 19 (Abstract); mixed-methods design, secondary datasets (COPASA 2003-2012, PNSB 2000/2008, IBGE Census 2000/2010), municipal sample restrictions (64 COPASA vs 256 municipal), Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney U tests, and qualitative interview sampling/analysis (n = 15) on PDF Pages 4-6 (Methodology, pp. 252-254); integrated quantitative-qualitative findings and measurement/confounding caveats on PDF Pages 6-14 (Results and Conclusions, pp. 254-262). Note: Tables 1-12 and Figures 1-8 were embedded as raster images in the source PDF so only their titles and sources appear in the text stream.

study_design_identified: Longitudinal observational panel (cohort) study of 527 special purpose public water districts in the Houston MSA (2008-2016, with lagged SDWA violations from 2005-2016) analysed with a two-part semi-continuous hierarchical Bayesian multilevel regression model
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study tracks an observational longitudinal panel of 527 special purpose water districts over fiscal years 2008-2016 to test whether lagged fiscal/economic capacity and prior 3-year SDWA regulatory violations predict subsequent annual debt issuance. Because there is no exogenous policy reform or assigned intervention evaluated with a quasi-experimental comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I), and because the data follow districts longitudinally across multiple years with lagged exposures and incomplete annual follow-up rather than a single cross-section (ruling out JBI Analytical Cross Sectional), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool.
selection_bias: Some concern: Within the target institutional forms (MUDs, FWSDs, WCIDs), coverage of the Houston MSA is nearly complete (527 of 533 active districts in 2016; Note 12, p. 14). However, defining the cohort via districts active in 2016 introduces survivorship bias by omitting districts active during 2008-2015 that consolidated, merged, or dissolved before 2016 (p. 12, Note 12 p. 14), and excluding municipal utilities (55% of regional population), private systems (4.5%), public corporations, and minor district types limits external generalizability across fragmented urban providers (pp. 3-4, 12, Note 9 p. 13).
measurement_bias: Some concern: Core variables come from official administrative registries (EPA SDWIS, TBRB bond database, TCEQ/TWDD financial audits, and GIS-weighted ACS census tract home values), avoiding recall bias. However, SDWA violations rely on utility self-monitoring (p. 3) where 8%-35% annual management/monitoring violation rates (p. 7) could mask undetected health violations; capital investment is proxied solely by new tax-exempt bond issuance, omitting cash/pay-as-you-go capital maintenance from operating revenues or fund slack (p. 10); fiscal slack combines modified-accrual fund balances with full-accrual net assets (p. 8, Note 7 p. 13); and default-zero customer counts use ad hoc carry-forward imputation (Table 1 Note a, p. 8).
confounding: Some concern (Moderate): Multilevel Bayesian models control for district random intercepts, fiscal-year random effects, system age, groundwater reliance, purchased water, statutory district type (MUD, WCID, FWSD), logged household equivalents, lagged outstanding debt, median home values, and management violations (pp. 6-8), supplemented by MUD-only and small-system subsample checks (Notes 9, 22). However, without a quasi-experimental design, unobserved confounders remain possible, including utility rate structures (unobserved, Note 10 p. 14), baseline physical infrastructure decay (p. 10), managerial expertise, developer financing cycles, and inter-district water transfer networks (p. 12).
attrition: Moderate-to-high concern: Among 527 included districts across fiscal years 2008-2016, complete nine-year audit follow-up was available for only 7 districts (1.3%), with 154 having eight audits, 207 having seven, 81 having six, and 78 having five or fewer audits; 3 active districts were dropped for unmatched audits and 1 audit for data error (Note 12, p. 14). Reasons for missing annual audits are not analysed, and no formal missing-data correction is applied beyond last-observation-carried-forward for default-zero customer unit counts (Table 1 Note a, p. 8).
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registration or pre-analysis protocol is reported. Full 95% posterior credible intervals for all four primary specifications are transparently reported in Figures 1-2 and Appendix Table A1 (pp. 9-11, 17), while robustness checks (1-5 year violation windows, violation counts, MUD-only, and small-system subsamples) are summarized narratively in footnotes without full tables (Notes 9, 13, 20-22). Minor internal reporting discrepancies appear (p. 2 states an eight-year period vs nine fiscal years 2008-2016 in Data/Note 12; Table A1 labels violation lags t-1:t-4 vs a 3-year window in text; Table 1 prints US$1.44N for median fund balance).
legal_measurement_quality: Strong-to-adequate: The study accurately operationalizes federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) compliance categories administered by TCEQ—distinguishing substantive health violations (contaminant and treatment technique failures) from procedural management violations (monitoring, reporting, and public notice)—and accounts for statutory distinctions across Texas Water Code Chapters 51, 53, and 54, small-system variance rules, and municipal allocation agreements (pp. 3-7, Notes 2-4, 8-10). However, binary 3-year violation indicators from EPA SDWIS depend on utility self-monitoring and do not capture violation severity or enforcement escalation.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate (with construct scope limitation): New tax-exempt debt issuance (binary incidence and dollar amount, excluding refinancing and filtered to 98% water-related plus 2% general/combined utility bonds) is measured objectively and reliably from the Texas Bond Review Board database (pp. 5-7, Note 8 p. 13). However, as a proxy for utility infrastructure investment, bond issuance excludes non-debt pay-as-you-go capital spending and state grant/loan financing, and the study measures financial response rather than subsequent resolution of drinking water quality violations.
where_found: Research design and statistical specification in 'Research design and methods' (PDF pp. 5-6) and 'Results' (PDF pp. 8-11, Figures 1-2, Appendix Table A1 p. 17); sampling frame, data linkage, variable definitions, and panel completeness in 'Background and case selection' (PDF pp. 2-4), 'Data' (PDF pp. 6-8, Table 1), and Endnotes 1-22 (PDF pp. 13-15); scope and network limitations in 'Implications for research and practice' (PDF p. 12).

study_design_identified: Multi-country repeated cross-sectional econometric study using spatial instrumental-variable (2SLS) quasi-experimental identification and OLS institutional moderation regressions (N = 142,838 households across 28 African countries, 2005-2015)
why_tool_chosen: Selected ROBINS-I per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study evaluates the causal impact of non-randomized spatial exposure to active and inactive mining operations (0-50 km and 50-100 km buffers relative to unexposed households) and local institutional governance using a quasi-experimental Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS / instrumental variables) identification strategy rather than a purely descriptive cross-sectional regression.
selection_bias: Moderate risk: Data come from nationally representative Afrobarometer survey rounds across 28 African countries (2005-2015; N = 142,838), which mitigates arbitrary sampling, but the repeated cross-sectional structure cannot account for selective residential migration into active mining zones or out-migration following mine closures, and sample construction/exclusion steps from raw survey waves are not documented.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: Mining exposure relies on a static inventory of 435 registered commercial mines that omits widespread unregistered artisanal/small-scale mines and lacks reported time-varying opening/closure dates across the 2005-2015 survey waves; furthermore, both household welfare outcomes and local governance moderators are derived from subjective self-reports in the same Afrobarometer survey, introducing common-source perception bias in the governance models.
confounding: Serious risk: Main mining models (Tables 2-3) use geological nonfuel mineral deposits within 0-50 km and 50-100 km as instruments with country and year fixed effects, but omit key geographic/hydrological confounders (river basins, elevation, precipitation, colonial transport corridors), suffer from weak instruments when separating active and inactive mines (Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F = 7.716), condition on potentially post-treatment mediators (employment, piped water, clinics, electricity), and rely on uninstrumented OLS/LPM regressions (Table 4) for the endogenous local governance moderation analysis.
attrition: No information: As a pooled repeated cross-sectional survey study rather than a longitudinal cohort, panel attrition does not apply, and the authors report zero information on survey non-response rates, geo-coding exclusions, or item-level missingness (such as 'don't know' responses on corruption or deprivation items) behind the 142,838 analytical sample.
reporting_bias: No information / Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is reported to verify pre-specification of the binary outcome cutoffs, 0-50 km and 50-100 km buffer thresholds, covariate sets, or governance interaction models, and minor reporting discrepancies appear in the published text and tables (e.g., Table 1 note citing Afrobarometer rounds 3-5 vs. text stating rounds 3-6; dropped minus signs in typeset Tables 2-4 compared with text interpretations).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak: Local institutional governance and environmental regulatory capacity are not measured using statutory provisions, mining licenses, or administrative enforcement records, but are proxied solely by regional averages of respondents' subjective Afrobarometer perceptions of local councillor corruption, tax official corruption, and local government disapproval; similarly, legal/formal mining status is inferred indirectly from 435 registered commercial mines in the World Bank Africa-PowerMining inventory without data on regulatory oversight or unregistered artisanal mining.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak: Household water security is operationalized solely via a dichotomized 12-month self-reported recall question ('gone without enough clean water for home use' at least once vs. never on a 0-4 scale), which captures perceived scarcity consistently across 28 countries but collapses frequency information and lacks any objective biophysical or chemical water-quality testing for invisible mining pollutants (e.g., heavy metals or acid mine drainage).
where_found: Data sources, variable definitions, descriptive statistics, and 2SLS econometric specification in 'DATA AND EMPIRICAL STRATEGY' (PDF pp. 4-8, Table 1); 2SLS main and active-vs-inactive mine estimates in 'THE EFFECT OF ACTIVE AND INACTIVE MINES: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE' (PDF pp. 8-10, Tables 2-3); local governance perception indicators and OLS interaction models in 'THE RELEVANCE OF LOCAL GOVERNANCE FOR THE EFFECTS OF MINING' (PDF pp. 10-13, Figures 1-2, Table 4); limitations on artisanal mining and exact Afrobarometer survey item wording in 'CONCLUSIONS' and 'ENDNOTES' (PDF pp. 13-14).

study_design_identified: Mixed-methods process evaluation conducted alongside a cluster-randomised controlled trial (combining qualitative semi-structured interviews and NGO/VWSC documentary reviews with longitudinal physical latrine observations, random-sample household and VWSC surveys, cluster-level arm comparisons, and village-level linear regressions)
why_tool_chosen: While connected to a 100-village cluster-randomised trial whose design and health-impact evaluation are reported elsewhere [6], this paper itself is a primary mixed-methods process evaluation combining qualitative data (semi-structured interviews with NGO staff, village motivators, and community members plus documentary logbook/register reviews) and quantitative data (longitudinal household latrine observations, 10% random-sample surveys of households and VWSC members, cluster-level comparisons, and ecological linear regressions). MMAT (with the Quantitative descriptive 4.1-4.5 block alongside Qualitative 1.1-1.5 and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5) is therefore the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (MMAT narrative judgment; overall quality constrained by weakest component: strong mixed-methods integration and objective latrine observation, but unreported qualitative coding/analysis, unreported survey response rates, incomplete motivator logs, and unadjusted ecological regressions)
selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: At the cluster level, 100 villages in Puri district were selected 'with government cooperation' (eligibility details deferred to protocol [6]) and randomly allocated 50:50 to intervention and control (Page 2). Within villages, the 10% household survey (n = 807) and 10% VWSC survey (n = 170) used random selection from village lists via Stata 13 (Pages 2-3), but sample sizes were based on logistical considerations, non-response/refusal rates are unreported, absent household heads were pragmatically substituted with any present household member aged >16 years (Page 2), and sampling for qualitative NGO/community interviews is not described.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Latrine construction status was measured rigorously through direct household inspection by independent enumerators every 6-8 weeks using explicit physical criteria (walls >1.5 m, door, unbroken/unblocked pan, functional pan-pipe-pit connection; Page 2), though assessors were unblinded and household denominators were distorted by joint families strategically over- or under-reporting splits depending on perceived subsidy benefits or cost contributions (Page 11). Mobilisation awareness relied on unvalidated self-report recall surveys (translated/back-translated into Oriya; Page 3), and delivery logs maintained by village motivators varied widely in completeness (Page 11).
confounding: Mixed (Low concern for randomized arm comparisons; High concern for within-arm ecological regressions): Comparisons of latrine construction progress (Figure 1) and awareness (Table 2) leverage the parent trial's 50:50 cluster randomization of 100 villages (balanced 8% baseline sanitation coverage; Page 4), though 49% of control households knew of the TSC via background exposure or spillover (Page 10). By contrast, the 13 village-level linear regressions within the 50 intervention villages (Table 4, Page 11) are non-randomized ecological analyses with zero adjustment for confounders (such as implementing NGO [coverage ranged 54%-76%], flood disruption in 13 villages, political unrest, or village poverty share).
attrition: Some concern / Can't tell: Across the 100 villages, assessed household totals shifted slightly from n = 4699 in March 2012 to n = 4585 in March 2013 (Figure 1, Page 6; ~2.4% change, complicated by fluctuating joint-family reporting noted on Page 11). However, response/refusal rates for the 10% household survey (n = 807) and 10% VWSC member survey (n = 170) are not reported, village motivator turnover disrupted record continuity (Page 11), and village-level fidelity data were missing for 2 villages on VWSCs, 7 villages on mapping, and 13 villages on Kumari committees (Pages 4, 7).
reporting_bias: Some concern: The parent cluster-RCT was registered (NCT01214785) with a published design protocol [6], and the authors candidly report implementation shortfalls and largely null associations. However, no pre-analysis plan is cited for the process evaluation regressions, qualitative interviews with community members mentioned in Methods (Page 2) are not systematically reported in Results, and minor internal discrepancies appear between text and tables (Page 7 text cites p = 0.02 for motivator home visits in the past month whereas Table 4 reports p = 0.05; Table 2 prints count difference 230 instead of percentage difference for home visits and lists n = 257 NGO visitors out of n = 242 home-visit respondents).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: The paper accurately outlines the policy architecture and operational rules of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC, 1999) and its 2012 successor Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA), including BPL vs APL subsidy rules, the June 2011 subsidy increase from INR 2200 to INR 3200, Nirmal Gram Puraskar open-defecation-free incentives, VWSC mandates, and election code-of-conduct pauses (Pages 2-5, 9-10). Crucially, it empirically separates de jure TSC guidelines from de facto implementation (e.g., universalising subsidies to APL households via WaterAid funds to prevent village conflict, Page 7), though it cites administrative guidelines rather than primary statutory instruments.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-good for latrine construction; absent for actual latrine use: Physical latrine construction status ('completed' vs 'under construction'/damaged) was directly observed across households using clear structural specifications (Page 2), notwithstanding household-unit boundary difficulties in joint-family compounds (Page 11). Awareness and participation outcomes relied on retrospective self-report over 1-12 months. Despite the title referencing 'latrine construction and use', actual behavioural latrine use or open-defecation behaviour was not measured in this paper.
where_found: PDF Pages 1-3 (Abstract and Methods: process evaluation objectives, 6-8 weekly monitoring rounds, physical latrine criteria, 10% random-sample household and VWSC surveys, Stata 13 village-level t-tests and linear regressions); Pages 3-11 (Results, Figures 1-2, Tables 1-4: context, TSC policy rules, fidelity, awareness, and coverage regressions); Pages 9-11 (Discussion: subsidy changes, floods, strategic household reporting, and incomplete motivator logbooks).

study_design_identified: Single-city political-economy and legal-institutional historical case study of municipal water service privatization contracts (1994-2011), supplemented by descriptive aggregate census tabulations (1990, 2005, 2010) and informal stakeholder correspondence
why_tool_chosen: Pierce (2012) is an institutional and political-economy historical case study analyzing municipal water concession/service governance, administrative restructuring (CADF to SACM), post-2003 contract renegotiation opacity, and transparency-law mobilization in Mexico City, accompanied only by a five-row descriptive summary table of aggregate INEGI census percentages (Table 3) and three cited personal communications. It is not a quasi-experimental comparative evaluation with statistical counterfactual estimation (ruling out ROBINS-I, which excludes descriptive single-case histories without econometric comparator analysis), not a unit-level analytical cross-sectional or cohort study (ruling out JBI checklists), not a primary qualitative interview/ethnographic study with participant recruitment and qualitative coding or a genuine primary mixed-methods design (ruling out CASP and MMAT), and not a systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly fits this institutional/legal-historical case study design.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (strong jurisdictional and institutional contextualization, adequate exposure/outcome description, weak sampling/coding transparency and weak causal/confounding control)
selection_bias: High concern: Documentary sources, news reports, corporate circulars, and the three personal-communication informants (SACM director, Suez/Bal-Ondeo representative, UNAM researcher; PDF p. 12 / p. 685) were purposively selected with no documented search strategy, inclusion criteria, or informant recruitment protocol, creating substantial risk of selective source inclusion for the opaque post-2003 period.
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Household access rates in Table 3 use standardized INEGI census categories (basic network access vs. in-home piped connection), though basic access conflates standpipes and piped supply; post-2003 contract performance, efficiency stagnation, and political 'disinformation' claims rely on secondary reports, news articles, corporate press releases, and informal correspondence without standardized measurement instruments (PDF pp. 5, 8, 11-13 / pp. 678, 681, 684-686).
confounding: High concern: Table 3 presents unadjusted census connection percentages across the DF, Outer ZMCM, Outer ZMVM, and Mexico with no statistical control for major confounders explicitly acknowledged in the text, including starkly different population growth rates (5% in DF vs. 52% in Outer ZMCM and 57% in Outer ZMVM), baseline ceiling effects in DF, different water-official tenure lengths (6-year vs. 3-year terms), urban in-migration, and aquifer depletion (PDF pp. 8-9 / pp. 681-682).
attrition: Low concern for aggregate INEGI census cross-sections (1990, 2005, 2010), which enumerate full municipal populations rather than a longitudinal cohort; however, severe post-2003 administrative reporting attrition occurred as SACM curtailed public disclosure of metering, customer-registry, and contract performance metrics (PDF p. 12 / p. 685).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No study protocol or pre-analysis plan exists; census comparisons report 1990, 2005, and 2010 while omitting 1995 and 2000 INEGI waves without explanation, and the Abstract and Conclusions assert unequivocally that privatization 'clearly improved the quality of the city's physical infrastructure and service provision' (PDF p. 14 / p. 687) despite earlier acknowledging that 'it is not entirely clear whether the improvements are attributable to service privatization' (PDF p. 9 / p. 682).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-weak: The study clearly delineates the 1994 four-zone private service/concession structure (Tables 1, 2, and 4), the institutional transition from CADF (1992) to SACM (2003), municipal tenure rules, and civil-society appeals under the 2002 Federal Transparency Law of Access to Public Information, but relies on secondary literature, press reports, and personal communications rather than primary contract texts, municipal decrees, or regulatory filings (partly due to SACM opacity post-2003).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Mixed: Aggregate household connection coverage is measured via national census waves (1990, 2005, 2010) held to consistent pre-2004 SEDESOL metropolitan boundaries (PDF pp. 5-6, 8 / pp. 678-679, 681), but census access indicators omit water quality, intermittency, pressure, and affordability, while post-2003 operational and equity outcomes rely on qualitative summaries of secondary audits (UNAM 2010) and media reports of rationing cutoffs.
where_found: Data and Methodology (PDF p. 5 / p. 678); Before Service Privatization & Privatization Structure (PDF pp. 5-7 / pp. 678-680, Tables 1-2); Impact of Service Privatization on Household Water Access (PDF pp. 7-9 / pp. 680-682, Table 3); Political Economy & Post-2003 Contract Renegotiations / Transparency Sections (PDF pp. 9-14 / pp. 682-687, Table 4); Conclusions & Notes (PDF pp. 14-15 / pp. 687-688).

study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental longitudinal municipal panel evaluation using difference-in-differences (DiD) fixed-effects regressions and propensity-score common-support trimming
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates the municipal-level causal effect of a non-randomized legal/institutional intervention (transferring water and sewerage service delivery from direct municipal provision to specialized corporate entities EICE or ESP under Colombia's Law 142 of 1994) against a genuine comparator group (municipalities retaining direct local government service provision) using panel difference-in-differences fixed-effects models and propensity-score common-support trimming (Sections 5-7, PDF pp. 6-10). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the designated appraisal tool for non-randomized comparative policy/intervention evaluations using DiD and propensity-score methods.
selection_bias: Serious concern: From 623 municipalities in the March 2007 SSPD registry, municipalities served by authorized rural/community organizations (329 for water) and marginal producers were excluded because they could not incorporate (Section 3(c), Table 1). Crucially, in the primary infectious-disease mortality DiD models (Table 4, Columns 3-4), observations were restricted to nonzero mortality values (dropping from 7,725 to 3,332 observations), directly conditioning sample inclusion on the post-intervention outcome.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Reform exposure is derived from a March 2007 SSPD administrative snapshot and water-service reform is used as a proxy for overall service reform in mortality models (Note 17). Outcomes come from national administrative sources (DANE Vital Statistics ICD-10 List 6/67 and 1993/2005 National Censuses), but the authors acknowledge documented underregistration of infant/child deaths in DANE Vital Statistics (Note 14), and census coverage measures household connection rates without capturing water potability, continuity, or treatment quality (Section 4(a)).
confounding: Serious concern: Reform adoption under Law 142 was endogenous and strongly associated with larger subscriber base (>2,500 subscribers), higher 1993 coverage, lower rurality, lower electoral turnout, and greater party fragmentation (Section 5, Table 3). Although municipality and year fixed effects, time-varying covariates, and propensity-score common-support trimming (0.07 to 0.95) mitigate time-invariant and baseline imbalances in Table 4, Figures 3 and 4 reveal markedly steeper pre-1994 mortality declines in non-reforming municipalities with no formal parallel-trends test or municipality-specific trends, and the coverage DiD models (Table 5) omit both time-varying controls and propensity-score trimming.
attrition: Serious concern: Out of 623 SSPD-registered municipalities (and >1,000 municipalities nationwide), the analytic sample drops from 550 eligible municipalities to 318 in the reform-adoption logit (Table 3) without explanation, to 515 (429 on common support) for non-external child mortality, to 380 (307 on common support) for infectious-disease mortality after excluding zero-death municipality-years, and to 484 municipalities (932 of 968 possible observations) in the census coverage regressions (Table 5). Underreporting of child deaths in DANE vital registration (Note 14) poses an additional missing-data risk.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported. Specification choices vary asymmetrically across outcomes (truncating zero-death observations in Columns 3-4 of Table 4 without showing full-sample sensitivity estimates; applying propensity-score common-support trimming and time-varying covariates in Table 4 but omitting them in Table 5; omitting sewerage-reform mortality regressions per Note 17), and published Tables 3-5 omit negative signs on coefficients that the text describes as negative.

study_design_identified: Sequential and longitudinal mixed-methods primary study combining residential ethnographic participant observation and key-informant interviews with a 5-wave (10-month) observational household panel survey of 72 randomly sampled households (plus 2008 follow-up interviews)
why_tool_chosen: The paper is a genuine primary mixed-methods empirical study that integrates qualitative ethnography (participant observation, key-informant interviews, and open-ended institutional analysis) with a quantitative 5-wave longitudinal household panel survey comparing seasonal exposure periods and community-membership tenure groups via t-tests and repeated-measures/split-plot ANOVAs. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, evaluating Screening S1–S2, Qualitative 1.1–1.5, Quantitative non-randomized 3.1–3.5, and Mixed-methods integration 5.1–5.5) is the exact matching instrument; purely qualitative (CASP), purely cross-sectional (JBI), and quasi-experimental intervention (ROBINS-I) checklists would each omit or mischaracterize core empirical components of the design.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (strong qualitative ethnography, random community sampling, and mixed-methods integration, tempered by ~20% unaddressed longitudinal panel attrition including scarcity-driven renter dropout, unadjusted quantitative analyses with political confounding, and binary self-report participation measures; no numeric composite score per MMAT 2018)
selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Within Villa Israel, households were randomly sampled from a complete community map of 415 residential constructions (96 contacted, 72 enrolled; 75% participation rate) and interviewed in Spanish, Quechua, or Aymara; however, Villa Israel was purposively selected as a single 'typical' south-side squatter settlement case study, and post-hoc selection of the most informative household respondent in 33% of multi-respondent households could introduce subtle within-household selection bias.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Household water insecurity was measured with a grounded 9-point Guttman scale (Hadley and Wutich 2009), but tapstand access, Neighborhood Council attendance, and food-sharing networks relied on 1-week retrospective self-reports subject to recall bias and social-desirability/deference effects (PDF p. 12 / p. 190); rule-breaking and sanctioning were severely underreported on the survey (only 4 admissions across >1,000 questions) and documented unsystematically via observation and second-hand reports (PDF p. 7 / p. 185), and respondent selection in 33% of households was finalized post hoc after wave 5 based on answer breadth/depth (PDF p. 4 / p. 182).
confounding: High concern / Serious risk: Quantitative comparisons across seasonal periods and between community members and non-community members rely exclusively on unadjusted cross-tabulations, bivariate t-tests, and unadjusted repeated-measures/split-plot ANOVAs without controlling for household size, income, length of residence, or physical proximity to an active tapstand; additionally, seasonal Neighborhood Council participation trends were severely confounded by a concurrent corruption scandal and impeachment movement against the Council president (PDF p. 9 / p. 187).
attrition: High concern / Moderate-to-serious risk: 72 of 96 randomly sampled households enrolled at baseline (75% response rate), but repeated-measures ANOVAs and t-tests report error degrees of freedom corresponding to only N=57–58 complete households (F(3,54), t(55), F(4,53), F(4,52)), indicating ~19–21% missing longitudinal panel data not accounted for in statistical analyses; moreover, a qualitative case vignette (PDF p. 10 / p. 188) documents differential attrition in which an impoverished renter family moved away before round 3 due to dry-season water and financial stress.
reporting_bias: Some concern / No pre-analysis plan: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is cited (expected for 2003–2005 anthropological fieldwork); full methodological details are cross-referenced to the author's 2006 PhD dissertation, only Wave 2–5 (four periods) are reported for the water-insecurity ANOVA (Table 3) versus five periods for tapstand, Council, and network analyses (Tables 4–8), and Table 5 contains an unexplained row-percentage anomaly in the Dry Season row.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong: Informal and customary urban property-tenure and common-pool water governance rules (landownership via loteador subdivision, family proxy occupancy, anticrético collateral-loan tenure, formal exclusion of renters, bimonthly 10-boliviano punch-card rules, 40 L to 20 L rationing, and four-tier monitoring/sanctioning) are richly documented ethnographically and explicitly operationalized in the survey Appendix (PDF pp. 5–7, 13 / pp. 183–185, 191), though municipal land-titling legalization status was not separately coded at the household level.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate: Household experiential water insecurity was measured systematically across seasons via a 9-item Guttman scale (Appendix, PDF pp. 12–13 / pp. 190–191) supplemented by separate diary estimates of per-capita water consumption (Table 2), whereas institutional outcomes (tapstand collection and Neighborhood Council attendance) were coarsened to binary past-week Yes/No indicators analyzed only descriptively, with an apparent percentage reporting discrepancy in Table 5 ('Dry season' row sums to 120.0%: 86.7% and 33.3%).

study_design_identified: Retrospective spatio-temporal ecological observational study (administrative utility billing panel and geospatial mixed-effects regression across 2,380 residential itineraries, 2008-2018, with cross-sectional household survey validation)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study is an observational ecological regression examining differences in billed per-capita domestic water consumption across administrative residential zoning categories (R1-R4) and settlement built-up eras without any policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental evaluation structure (ruling out ROBINS-I) and without following outcome-free cohorts for incident outcomes (ruling out JBI Cohort Studies). Although monthly meter readings span 2008-2018, the primary exposures (residential zoning class and GHS built-up period) are static spatial classifications analyzed via a negative binomial regression with year as a random intercept and validated cross-sectionally against KSCBS household data, making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies the closest-fitting instrument.
selection_bias: High concern: The study frame is restricted to NCWSC piped water billing itineraries, systematically excluding informal and newly settled residential neighbourhoods outside the municipal piped network, and additionally excludes 554 itineraries (including 92 residential itineraries) lacking geographical coordinates without comparing included versus excluded areas.
measurement_bias: High concern: Outcome per-capita domestic consumption divides NCWSC billed meter volumes by WorldPop random-forest modelled grid populations, omitting 29% non-revenue water (including illegal connections, leaks, and irregular/unmetered connections), omitting alternative water sources (vendors, boreholes, tankers), and conflating residential economic/commercial water use with domestic consumption. Exposure zoning categories rely on coarse built-environment/land-use proxies with an abrupt 2013 population shift between R1 and R4.
confounding: High concern: The multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model adjusts for only three ecological covariates (residential zoning category, built-up settlement age, and modelled itinerary population, plus a random effect for year) due to unavailable small-area census statistics. Unmeasured household socio-economic heterogeneity, commercial/productive water use within residential connections, private water storage capacity, and off-grid water sources create substantial residual confounding and ecological fallacy risk.
attrition: Moderate concern / Unclear: 554 itineraries (including 92 residential itineraries) were dropped at the outset due to missing geographical coordinates; reservoir water production metering was only available from November 2016 to May 2018 due to meter breakages; rationing schedules were restricted to October 2016-December 2018; and the completeness of monthly customer meter readings across the 132 months (2008-2018) per itinerary is not reported.
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and multivariable covariate selection relied on univariable p < 0.2 screening. Several internal numerical inconsistencies appear in the published text and tables, including mismatched itinerary filtering counts/percentages (PDF Page 5), a reversed inequality sign for 2018 R4 density in Table 2 (<18,000), low-income built-up subgroup counts summing to 263 versus 252 total in Table 4, and an incompatible p-value (0.425) for a rate ratio of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.53-0.56) in Table 4.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Official administrative residential zoning classifications (R1-R4 derived from the 1973 Master Plan / 1985 water distribution plans and updated via the 2014 Nairobi Integrated Urban Development Master Plan), NCWSC domestic block tariffs (2015-2018), and formal weekly rationing schedules (2016-2018) are sourced directly from utility and ministry records and cross-validated against KSCBS tenure/slum indicators, though informal land-use transitions, an unexplained sharp 2013 reclassification shift, and unenforced private kiosk retail pricing introduce administrative proxy error.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (high risk of measurement error): While water sufficiency uses Gleick's standard >1500 L/capita/month benchmark, numerator data come solely from billed utility customer meters (missing unbilled/illegal consumption within the 29% non-revenue water loss and all non-piped water sources, while including small-scale commercial uses) and denominator data rely on dasymetric gridded population projections that include unpiped residents within itinerary boundaries and mask intra-itinerary household inequality.
where_found: Methods and data sources on PDF Pages 3-6 (Sections 2.1-2.3); descriptive, rationing, and regression results on PDF Pages 6-10 (Sections 3.1-3.3.1, Tables 1-4, Supplemental Table 1A, Figures 1-6); methodological limitations on PDF Page 11 (Section 4 Discussion).

study_design_identified: Multi-essay observational econometric dissertation without a quasi-experimental intervention structure: Essay 1 uses state-year panel regressions and a Random Effects Spatial Durbin Model (48 U.S. states, 2000-2011, N=576); Essay 2 uses pooled cross-sectional spatial hedonic and 2SLS spatial quantile regressions of single-family home sales linked to prior-year boil water notices (Marion County, WV, 2012-2017, N=1,985); Essay 3 uses cross-sectional OLS regression of residential water charges across 110 West Virginia public service districts.
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: All three essays are observational econometric regressions examining environmental/regulatory exposures or utility characteristics without an exogenous policy rollout or quasi-experimental intervention comparator—explicitly confirmed by the author in Essay 2 ('Since we are not employing a quasi-experimental identification strategy in this study', PDF p. 91). Essay 2 (pooled cross-sectional hedonic regression of 1,985 property sales) and Essay 3 (cross-sectional OLS of 110 public service districts) are cross-sectional observational regressions, and even Essay 1's 2000-2011 state panel relies primarily on between-state Random Effects variation (with null within-state two-way fixed effects) using continuous SDWA violation rates as a proxy for water contamination rather than evaluating a discrete policy intervention. Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the best-fitting instrument over ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Moderate concern: Essay 1 includes all 48 contiguous U.S. states from 2000 to 2011 for public water systems, but excludes ~45 million residents using private wells outside SDWA jurisdiction (PDF p. 43). Essay 2 applies transparent arm's-length filtering to Marion County Assessor records (7,972 sales -> 5,525 with structures -> 1,985 arm's-length single-family sales, 2013-2017; PDF pp. 86, 89-90), though 17% of county structures lack public water service and ~5% of residents use private wells (PDF pp. 84-85) without explicit parcel-level exclusion of non-networked homes. Essay 3 analyzes 110 West Virginia public service districts (PDF p. 4), but detailed sampling/exclusion criteria in Section 4.5 lie in the truncated tail of the PDF (pp. 103-180).
measurement_bias: High concern for exposure measurement; Low concern for outcome measurement: In Essay 1, the author notes that EPA estimated states failed to report 40% of health-based SDWA violations (U.S. EPA, 2004; PDF p. 43), state-level aggregation averages out localized contamination, private wells (~45 million U.S. residents) are excluded, and within-year repeat exposures and multi-year lags are omitted. In Essay 2, 90 of 440 BWNs (20.5%) in Marion County could not be used due to missing affected street/area details (54 BWNs) or missing lift dates (36 BWNs) (PDF p. 87), misclassifying affected homes during those episodes as unexposed. Conversely, outcomes (CMS NHEA real per capita Personal Health Care spending, Marion County Assessor arm's-length sale prices, and regulated PSD water charges per 4,500 gallons) come from standardized official records.
confounding: Moderate-to-high concern: None of the three essays uses a quasi-experimental causal design, as explicitly stated in Essay 2 (PDF p. 91). Essay 1 controls for state GDP, unemployment, uninsured rate, BRFSS health status, Medicare share, natural resource spending, air quality nonattainment, hospital beds, year fixed effects, and spatial lags, but relies on Random Effects despite a significant Hausman test favoring Fixed Effects, and in non-spatial two-way state and year fixed-effects models the SDWA violation coefficient vanishes (0.000, p = 0.910; PDF pp. 32, 67). Essay 2 mitigates observable and time-invariant spatial confounding via structural quality/condition grades, GIS proximity/neighborhood controls, tax-district (and census block-group) fixed effects, sale-year fixed effects, spatial lag models, and 2SLS spatial quantile regression, though unobserved localized infrastructure shocks within tax districts remain possible. Essay 3 uses cross-sectional OLS across 110 utilities (full chapter truncated).
attrition: Low concern (with item-level administrative missingness in Essay 2): Essay 1 uses a balanced panel of all 48 contiguous U.S. states from 2000 to 2011 (N = 576, zero state-year attrition; PDF pp. 25, 67). Essay 2 analyzes cross-sectional arm's-length property sales rather than a longitudinal cohort, though 90 of 440 Marion County boil water notices (20.5%) were dropped due to missing location or lift-date records (PDF p. 87). Essay 3 is cross-sectional (N = 110 public service districts; full chapter truncated after PDF p. 102).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan): As an observational PhD dissertation without a pre-analysis plan, specification flexibility exists across functional forms, spatial weight matrices, and random-vs-fixed effects choices. Positively, the author transparently reports null results, including null two-way FE/RE non-spatial estimates for SDWA violations in Essay 1 (Table 2.3, PDF p. 67), null air-pollution effects (Table 2.4, PDF p. 68), unreported insignificant 1-month BWN models noted in Footnote 11 (PDF p. 89), null BWN effects at upper housing price quantiles (>= 0.7; PDF p. 101), and null NRCS impoundment rate differences in Essay 3 (Abstract, PDF p. 4). However, emphasizing the Random Effects Spatial Durbin Model in Essay 1 after non-spatial state+year FE yielded a zero point estimate warrants caution.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate with administrative reporting gaps: Essay 1 accurately distinguishes Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based violations (MCL, MRDL, TT) from monitoring/reporting violations under state primacy rules (PDF pp. 21-23), operationalizing annual population share served by non-compliant public water systems, but suffers from ecological state aggregation and ~40% state non-reporting to EPA SDWIS (PDF p. 43). Essay 2 geocodes and street-matches 350 official WV OEHS / Marion County Health Department Boil Water Notices across four exposure metrics (count, days, average duration, binary indicator in the prior year; PDF pp. 85-90), weakened by 90 unlinked notices. Essay 3 frames multi-source water utility rate comparisons around West Virginia Senate Bill 373 (2014 Source Water Protection Act; PDF pp. 4, 13), but measures physical raw water source configurations rather than statutory compliance directly (full Chapter 4 truncated).
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong / High for economic and expenditure outcomes (indirect for human health in Essay 1): Essay 1 uses official CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts real per capita Personal Health Care spending by state of residence deflated by the PHC price index (PDF pp. 25-27), while explicitly noting that health care expenditures do not directly measure health status outcomes (PDF p. 26). Essay 2 uses official Marion County Assessor arm's-length single-family transaction prices (N = 1,985; PDF p. 86). Essay 3 uses standardized residential water charges per 4,500 gallons across 110 WV public service districts (PDF p. 4).

study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional geospatial observational study (secondary spatial/administrative analysis comparing irrigation districts across historical formation eras/clusters and comparing disadvantaged communities inside vs. outside irrigation district boundaries at a single contemporary cross-section)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The empirical analysis compiles cross-sectional spatial and administrative indicators (2016 Land IQ crop composition/revenue, multi-year average surface water deliveries collapsed into a single cross-sectional district metric, and 2018 DWR/CalEnviroScreen 4.0 community indicators) to perform observational cross-sectional comparisons across irrigation district formation eras/clusters and between ID-DACs (n = 97) and GDCs (n = 56) using descriptive statistics and unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon tests. Because there is no longitudinal panel tracking of outcomes over time and no quasi-experimental intervention evaluation structure (such as DiD, RDD, IV, ITS, or matching), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool rather than ROBINS-I or JBI Cohort.
selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern — the study covers the full census of agricultural irrigation districts and all 153 DWR-mapped 2018 DAC census places (97 ID-DACs and 56 GDCs) on the San Joaquin Valley floor across eight counties, avoiding survey non-response; however, excluding domestic, municipal, and water conservation agencies while classifying all DACs outside agricultural irrigation districts as "groundwater-dependent communities" creates structural frame misclassification regarding domestic water service.
measurement_bias: High concern — groundwater reliance is not measured from metered pumping but inferred as a simplified steady-state water-budget residual combining asynchronous periods (2001–2015, 2005–2019, or 2008–2019 average surface deliveries minus 2016 Land IQ/WAFR crop evapotranspiration demand), imputing "no record" deliveries as zero; additionally, census-tract CalEnviroScreen 4.0 percentiles are linked to DAC census places via spatial centroids, and GDCs are defined solely by falling outside agricultural irrigation districts without verifying municipal/domestic water system service.
confounding: High concern — no confounding variables were controlled for in either the historical-era irrigation district comparisons or the ID-DAC (n = 97) vs. GDC (n = 56) comparisons. Bivariate Wilcoxon tests do not adjust for substantial baseline differences such as population size (mean 9,899 in ID-DACs vs. 20,515 in GDCs, p = 0.0035), municipal incorporation, presence of domestic/municipal drinking-water utilities, aquifer hydrogeology, or spatial clustering across counties.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable for panel attrition (secondary cross-sectional spatial census of districts and DAC places); however, missing administrative records introduce bias because irrigation districts with "no record" of surface water delivery were imputed as zero delivery rather than analyzed for missingness, and Kings County LAFCO lacked updated boundary files (relying on 2015 DWR boundaries).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern — no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported, formal statistical tests across the four historical formation eras are omitted, and the clustering algorithm, distance metric, and cluster-count selection criteria for the 5-group typology (Section 3.4, Fig 5) are not specified in the manuscript text, although underlying datasets and R scripts are publicly archived on Dryad and GitHub.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern — legal/institutional classifications (Wright Act of 1887, pre-1914 senior vs. post-1914 SWRCB appropriative water rights, SGMA, and LAFCO irrigation district boundaries) draw on official state/local registries (LAFCO, eWRIMS, USBR contracts, GSPs, AWMPs) verified with district managers, but surface water rights are modeled at 100% face allocation, "no record" deliveries are assumed zero, Kings County uses older 2015 DWR boundaries, and agricultural irrigation district boundaries are conflated with local drinking-water governance despite excluding domestic and municipal water agencies.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-high concern — district groundwater reliance is an unvalidated modeled residual ignoring storage change, conveyance/recharge losses, and lateral groundwater flow, while community drinking-water and environmental outcomes rely on census-tract screening percentiles (2018 OEHHA CalEnviroScreen 4.0) joined to DAC place centroids rather than direct community water-system quality or household access measurements.
where_found: Study design, data sources, inclusion/exclusion rules, water-budget modeling assumptions, spatial centroid joins, and statistical tests are reported in Section 2 (Materials and methods, PDF Pages 6–10), with empirical comparisons, Table 1, and cluster profiles in Section 3 (Results and discussion, PDF Pages 10–16) and data/agency verification notes on PDF Pages 1 and 18.

study_design_identified: Institutional and legal-historical case study (single-country descriptive policy, statutory, and administrative synthesis of Ghana's water pricing and water sector reforms, 1965-2002)
why_tool_chosen: The paper is not a randomized trial, quasi-experimental comparative evaluation with a comparator arm (single-country history cannot be forced into ROBINS-I), cross-sectional/cohort analytical study, primary qualitative interview/ethnographic study, mixed-methods primary study, or systematic review. Instead, it is a single-jurisdiction institutional and legal-historical case study combining primary Ghanaian water statutes and legislative instruments with secondary administrative performance data from government and donor reports, which directly matches the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Strong descriptive legal-institutional documentation, but weak empirical rigor / high risk of bias for causal inference
selection_bias: High concern (weak selection transparency): No formal sampling frame or source selection protocol is reported; illustrative regions, irrigation schemes (e.g., Tono/Vea, Weija, Upper East, Eastern Region, 41 rural communities), and unpublished donor/agency reports are selected narratively.
measurement_bias: High concern (weak measurement transparency): Sector performance metrics (coverage rates, Unaccounted For Water, handpump maintenance recovery, and informal vendor water expenditure claims) are drawn from secondary government and donor reports without primary verification or consistent denominators; the authors themselves note that 1992 vs. 1998/1999 urban and rural coverage figures are non-comparable due to small-town transfers and settlement population threshold changes (5,000 vs. 15,000).
confounding: High concern (weak control): Institutional and tariff reforms are described chronologically alongside major concurrent shocks—including the Economic Recovery Programme/Structural Adjustment Programme, high inflation, a US$240 million donor-financed Water Sector Rehabilitation Project, loan-to-grant conversions, and cross-debt clearing—without any analytical strategy to separate legal/pricing effects from macroeconomic and capital-investment confounders.
attrition: Not assessable / Not applicable: This is a single-country institutional and legal-historical policy synthesis reporting aggregate national and sub-sector administrative figures rather than tracking a cohort or panel of sampled units over time.
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No pre-specified protocol, search strategy, or source inclusion criteria exist, and institutional insiders synthesize grey agency documents selectively under 'Achievements/Successes'; however, this risk is partially tempered by candid reporting of persistent failures such as 50-57% Unaccounted For Water, government bill defaults, delayed tariff approvals, and non-comparable coverage declines.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong-to-adequate: Primary Ghanaian statutes and legislative instruments governing water tariffs and sector governance are accurately identified by instrument number, year, and mandate (Act 310 of 1965 s. 2(2)(f), SMCD 85 of 1977, L.I. 1350 of 1987, L.I. 1597 of 1995, Act 522 of 1996, Act 538 of 1997), although de facto administrative compliance and enforcement are recounted narratively rather than measured systematically.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-adequate: Concrete administrative indicators (tariff schedules in cedis and US$, GWSC staffing, Unaccounted For Water, boreholes/hand-dug wells/latrines built, and urban/rural coverage percentages) are reported and key definitional breaks in coverage series are candidly flagged, but underlying survey/audit methods are omitted and key affordability assertions (e.g., low-income consumers paying >10 times official rates and >10% of income) lack cited empirical documentation.
where_found: Appraisal grounded across the full article (PDF pp. 2-9): Abstract and Introduction (PDF p. 2); History of Water Pricing in Ghana and Experiences in Water Pricing (PDF pp. 2-5); The Reform Process and Achievements/Successes (PDF pp. 5-7); Future Perspectives and Conclusion (PDF pp. 7-9); About the Authors and References (PDF p. 9). No standalone Methods section is present.

study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal panel evaluation (two-way fixed-effects and Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models of 208 urban water utilities in 192 Chinese cities, 1998-2007)
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a non-randomized institutional/policy intervention—private sector participation (partial or majority nonstate equity ownership) versus continued pure state ownership in urban water utilities—using comparative longitudinal panel econometrics (two-way fixed effects and Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluations with a genuine policy comparator map to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Moderate risk: The sample restricts NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys (annual sales > 5 million CNY) to large and medium-sized utilities in prefecture-level cities—excluding small county/town utilities and defining size via employment, assets and sales—and uses manual matching across firm ID changes (often triggered by ownership restructuring) to add 60 utilities into a 208-utility panel that also retains 9 prevalent PSP utilities already privatized by 1998 (PDF pp. 6-7, 12, Section III & Table 1).
measurement_bias: Moderate risk: Operationalizing PSP strictly from utility capital structure misclassifies cities using BOT, TOT or facility divestiture concessions into the state-owned comparator group, exhibits 27 three-year back-and-forth switching anomalies attributed to potential capital coding errors, and maps city-wide yearbook water supply aggregates onto individual utilities even in multi-utility municipalities (PDF pp. 7-8, 11, 15, 23-25, 27, 32).
confounding: Serious risk: Two-way fixed effects (utility and year), 1-year lagged utility and city controls, Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM, and a city-wide industrial profitability falsification test address time-invariant heterogeneity and observed lagged selection (such as prior profitability and road infrastructure). However, unobserved time-varying factors—including municipal leadership turnover, investor networks, and unmeasured local contractual guarantees on purchase volumes or tariff adjustments—simultaneously drive bidirectional PSP entry/exit and utility performance (PDF pp. 13-15, 17-20, 25, 31).
attrition: Serious risk: While the utility financial panel is nearly balanced (~2,072 utility-year observations across 208 utilities), employment data are completely missing for 2004, and regressions for urban domestic water supply and domestic water supply population in Table 8 drop to N = 814 (over 53% missingness relative to the N = 1,752 total urban water supply model and over 60% relative to the full panel) using complete-case analysis without missingness diagnostics (PDF pp. 7, 13, 22, 30).
reporting_bias: No information (some concern): No pre-analysis plan or study protocol exists. Although the authors report full estimates across 12 financial indicators and 3 city water supply indicators under both raw and post-hoc corrective coding in Tables 5-8, narrative conclusions foreground preferred corrective-recoded specifications where profit-sales ratio and 10%-level domestic water user effects reach statistical significance (PDF pp. 22-31).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: The authors accurately situate national regulatory milestones (1992 pilot opening, 2001 State Planning Committee guidelines, 2002 Ministry of Construction Circular No. 272 and 2004 Decree No. 126) and measure PSP via actual paid-in capital shares (>0% nonstate and >50% majority thresholds) rather than noisier enterprise registration labels. However, equity-share coding omits contractual PSP modes (BOT, TOT and facility divestiture), pools state-affiliated legal-entity capital with private capital, and cannot observe municipal concession terms or guaranteed-return/volume clauses (PDF pp. 7-11, 13-14, 31-32).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to Moderate: Utility financial and productivity indicators come from standardized NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys, though SOE versus private accounting incentives may affect reported managerial expenses and profits. Water service outcomes rely entirely on coarse city-level yearbook aggregates (total urban water supply, urban domestic water supply and imputed domestic users derived by dividing domestic supply by per-capita use) with severe missingness and no direct measurement of water quality, pressure, nonrevenue water/leakage or retail tariffs (PDF pp. 8-9, 27, 30-32).
