study_design_identified: Cross-sectional comparative mail survey of members in two purposively selected Public Water Supply Districts (with retrospective self-reported pre/post comparisons and no untreated control group)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The empirical data come from a single-wave quantitative mail questionnaire sent to members of two Missouri Public Water Supply Districts (Boone County PWSD No. 5 and Barton County PWSD No. 1), comparing descriptive means and percentages across district types (rural-urban fringe vs. agricultural) and residential/farm property subgroups. Because both surveyed districts received the PWSD intervention and there is no untreated control arm or quasi-experimental longitudinal/before-after identification strategy, ROBINS-I does not apply; the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
selection_bias: High concern: Two out of 88 operational Missouri PWSDs were purposively selected as illustrative rural-urban fringe and agricultural cases without random sampling or untreated comparison areas. Within those two districts, the 65% mail return rate (35% non-response) is acknowledged by the authors as likely reflecting respondents' positive valuation of district water services, indicating probable pro-intervention response bias, compounded by post-service in-migrants (40% in Boone, 25% in Barton) entering the sample.
measurement_bias: High concern: Pre- and post-district water consumption, hauled and pumped water unit costs, migration motives, home improvement expenditures, and land value appreciation were all measured via retrospective respondent recall and subjective estimation on a single mail questionnaire, without independent verification from district meter/billing records or bona fide real estate sales registries.
confounding: High concern: Although the authors explicitly identify major confounders—including an 18-month longer operating duration in Boone County PWSD No. 5, higher household income and younger household heads in Boone County, and concurrent regional pull factors (transportation, communications, schools, natural gas, and non-farm employment)—no untreated control communities/households were surveyed and no multivariable or statistical adjustment was performed.
attrition: High concern: Survey non-response was 35% in both districts (211 of 317 families responded in Boone County PWSD No. 5; 448 of 700 responded in Barton County PWSD No. 1), and item non-response was severe on key outcomes—45% of Boone respondents did not answer the land-price question, and only 66 of 448 Barton respondents estimated a percentage land-value increase. Prior residents who moved out before the survey were also unobservable.
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-analysis protocol or copy of the mail questionnaire is provided, and outcome reporting is asymmetric across districts—for instance, the exact count of respondents making home improvements is reported for Boone County (25 respondents averaging $1,126) but omitted for Barton County ('a number of respondents' averaging $672), and subgroup comparisons lack sample sizes and variance estimates.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak: Missouri's 1935 PWSD enabling statute, Regional Planning Commission construction authorization (described as largely a formality), and post-1961 Farmers Home Administration loan financing are noted only as institutional background. While district membership itself is administratively defined via district rolls, legal-institutional rules, rate structures, and service-boundary provisions are not systematically operationalized or coded.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Quantitative water use (monthly gallons), water unit prices, facility expenditure totals, and land price changes rely entirely on unvalidated self-reports with high item missingness, inconsistent subgroup denominators across districts, and zero dispersion metrics (no standard deviations or confidence intervals).
where_found: Study design and mail survey response rates: PDF p. 3 (journal p. 95, Footnote 2) and PDF p. 4 (journal p. 96, 'Overview of Districts Studied'). District settings, sample sizes, and demographics: PDF pp. 4-5 (journal pp. 96-97). Confounders and operating-duration caveats: PDF p. 5 (journal p. 97, text and Footnote 4) and PDF p. 8 (journal p. 100, 'Comparative Impacts'). Empirical results and self-reported outcome limitations: PDF pp. 5-8 (journal pp. 97-100, including PDF p. 6 / journal p. 98, Footnote 5). Institutional background: PDF p. 3 (journal p. 95, 'Historical Backdrop' and Footnote 1).

study_design_identified: Descriptive mixed-methods urban poverty-mapping survey and uncontrolled pilot programme report (combining a city-wide community/key-informant quantitative survey of 1,537 poverty pockets across four cities with participatory qualitative exercises in 24 slums, plus uncontrolled administrative output reporting for a 65-slum water and sanitation pilot)
why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary empirical data combining a quantitative descriptive component (city-wide structured PPSA questionnaires across 1,537 poverty pockets summarized in Table 1, plus descriptive SESI programme output counts across ~65 slums) and a qualitative component (key informant interviews, group discussions, and separate participatory exercises across six poverty pockets in each of the four cities) with an explicit triangulation rationale (PDF p. 4, p. 582). Because there is no comparator group or quasi-experimental evaluation structure for SESI, ROBINS-I does not apply; instead, MMAT (2018) using the Qualitative (1.1-1.5), Quantitative Descriptive (4.1-4.5), and Mixed-Methods (5.1-5.5) blocks is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: High methodological concern / Low overall quality (per MMAT 2018 narrative guidance, no numeric composite score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: mixed-methods triangulation rationale and integration are strong [5.1-5.4 Yes], but both the qualitative strand [1.4 No; 1.2, 1.3, 1.5 Can't tell] and the quantitative descriptive strand [4.2-4.5 Can't tell] have major reporting and measurement deficits, yielding 5.5 No)
selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: For the PPSA mapping component, attempting a city-wide census of all notified and non-notified poverty pockets across four cities (1,537 PPs in Table 1, PDF p. 5) reduced administrative exclusion of informal settlements, though operational thresholds for defining a 'poverty pocket' are unreported; selection of the 24 PPs (6 per city) for qualitative participatory exercises and ~65 PPs for the SESI intervention was purposive/consultative with municipal corporations and NGOs without transparent reproducible selection rules (PDF pp. 3-4, 7, 9).
measurement_bias: High concern: PPSA quantitative estimates in Table 1 were explicitly 'not a household survey' and relied on key informant interviews and group discussions recorded on questionnaires co-signed by municipal corporation officials and partner NGOs (PDF p. 2, p. 3), creating substantial risk of informant estimation error and institutional desirability bias; SESI outcomes (e.g., 60 open-defecation-free slums, 20,000 families with household toilets, PDF p. 10) are self-reported by an advisor of the implementing agency (UN-HABITAT) without operational definitions or independent verification.
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): Both the city-wide PPSA survey and the SESI pilot report are purely descriptive with no control/comparison slums or statistical adjustment, making it impossible to separate claimed SESI improvements from concurrent US$400 million ADB city-wide water and sanitation investments or DFID Madhya Pradesh Urban Services Project activities in the same four cities (PDF p. 2, p. 7).
attrition: Can't tell / No information: No pocket-level or household-level nonresponse rates are reported for the PPSA or baseline KAP surveys, and the discrepancy between the ~65 target SESI slums (PDF p. 7, p. 8) and the 60 open-defecation-free slums / 63 active Community Water and Sanitation Committees reported at project end (PDF p. 10) is not explained.
reporting_bias: High concern: Although the text states that household-level baseline water, sanitation, and hygiene KAP surveys were conducted in selected intervention slums (PDF p. 2, p. 4, p. 8), zero household survey data or pre-post comparisons are reported; furthermore, the data-collection flowchart on PDF p. 4 is missing/blank in the text layer and SESI evaluation findings consist solely of favourable summary outputs reported by a UN-HABITAT Regional Advisor without conflict-of-interest or reflexivity disclosure.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak: While the article centrally distinguishes officially recognised ('notified') slums and Below Poverty Line (BPL) households from 'non-notified slums' omitted from Census and municipal records (PDF p. 3, p. 5, p. 11, p. 13), it cites no statutory or municipal notification criteria, defines no operational verification rule for notification or BPL status, and does not disaggregate Table 1 by legal notification status.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: PPSA water and sanitation access percentages rely on community/informant estimates rather than direct household inspection or water-quality testing, although participatory qualitative inquiry usefully exposes why nominal infrastructure indicators overstate effective access (PDF p. 2, pp. 5-6); SESI intervention outcomes are presented only as rounded administrative output counts and unsubstantiated narrative claims without baseline denominators or independent audit (PDF pp. 10-11).
where_found: Introduction and study overview: PDF pp. 1-2 (pp. 579-580); Poverty Mapping Framework (PPSA) background, objectives, NGO/municipal mobilisation, survey/qualitative triangulation process, Table 1, and mixed-methods results: PDF pp. 2-7 (pp. 580-585; note embedded flowchart graphic on PDF p. 4 / p. 582 has no text layer); Slum Environmental Sanitation Initiative (SESI) background, objectives, activities, output counts, strategic impacts, sustainability, and lessons learnt: PDF pp. 7-13 (pp. 585-591).

study_design_identified: Quantitative cross-sectional household survey (community-level census of 232 consenting household heads in Cristais, Ceara, supplemented by secondary 2010 IBGE Census tabulations and direct field observation)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The primary empirical study in this paper is a single-wave quantitative cross-sectional household questionnaire survey (232 households in Cristais, May-July 2014) analyzing descriptive distributions and bivariate socioeconomic inequalities in water access without an active intervention or analyzed comparator arm. Although PDF p. 5 notes that Cristais was chosen as part of the broader DESAFIO project for future before-and-after evaluation and mentions a nearby control community with a WSS, this paper reports only baseline cross-sectional data from Cristais alone (ruling out ROBINS-I), and contains no formal qualitative interview/coding methodology beyond brief contextual observation (ruling out CASP and MMAT). Thus, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool.
selection_bias: Some concern: Surveying all consenting household heads in Cristais (232 questionnaires, PDF p. 3) mitigates within-community random sampling error, but the total number of eligible households in the community and refusal/non-contact counts are not reported, and the community itself was purposively selected because it lacked a WSS and was scheduled to receive a DESAFIO project intervention (PDF p. 5).
measurement_bias: High concern: Both socioeconomic stratifiers (household income) and water access outcomes (weekly water volume by source, collection trip time, payments to carroceiros) were obtained via self-reported household head questionnaires without independent volumetric metering, receipt verification, or timed observation (PDF pp. 3-4, 12-14), and water quality/pollution claims relied on resident perceptions rather than physicochemical or microbiological testing (PDF p. 11).
confounding: High concern: Macro- and micro-contextual determinants (income, schooling, sex, skin color, seasonality) are discussed conceptually (PDF pp. 7, 15), but the primary Cristais survey analysis presents only univariate distributions and one unadjusted bivariate breakdown of water expenditure share by total household income bracket (Figure 3, PDF p. 14), with zero adjustment for confounders such as household size, spatial distance to collective cisterns/canal, or occupation.
attrition: High concern (item missingness): Although cross-sectional with no longitudinal attrition, per capita water consumption excluded 39 of 232 surveyed households (n = 193 analyzed, 16.8% exclusion; misstated due to an arithmetic typo as '93 of the 232' in Note ii, PDF p. 16) because households could not estimate volumes from at least one water source—likely non-random missingness linked to unmetered hosepipe or surface-water abstraction.
reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-analysis plan or protocol registration is reported. Notably, PDF p. 5 notes that Cristais was selected for pre/post evaluation alongside a nearby control community with an operating WSS 'to test our hypothesis', yet no control-community data are reported in this article; additionally, Note ii (PDF p. 16) contains an arithmetic discrepancy ('reduced to 193 because 93 of the 232 households... were excluded', whereas 232 - 193 = 39).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (descriptive/normative operationalization): Accurately cites Brazilian Sanitation Act No. 11.445/2007, PLANSAB, Water Resources Act No. 9.433/1997, Ministry of Health Portaria No. 2914/2011, ARCE/CAGECE social and regular tariffs, and UN 2010 Human Right to Water resolutions (PDF pp. 1, 4, 6, 10-11, 14, 16-17) to define piped WSS absence and benchmark affordability/accessibility; however, legal-institutional exclusion from the Integration Canal is documented contextually at the community level rather than measured as a household-level legal exposure variable.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Conceptual operationalization is strong—capturing multidimensional Human Right to Water quantity, physical accessibility, and economic accessibility against Howard & Bartram (2003), JMP, and UNDP (2006) benchmarks (PDF pp. 4, 12-14)—but empirical measurement relies entirely on recall-based self-report, omits objective water-quality testing, and excludes 16.8% of surveyed households unable to quantify volumes from all sources (Note ii, PDF p. 16).
where_found: Methods, sampling, and outcome definitions are reported in Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 3-5) and Notes i-viii (PDF pp. 16-17); legal/institutional context and secondary IBGE 2010 Census comparisons are in Section 2 (PDF pp. 5-11); primary Cristais cross-sectional survey results are in Section 3 (PDF pp. 11-15) and Section 4 (PDF pp. 15-16), with English/Portuguese/Spanish abstracts on PDF pp. 21-22 (note: Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-3 are embedded images in the PDF, while full prose and key subgroup figures are reported in text).

study_design_identified: Cross-sectional comparative household survey (n = 652; 331 WRUA members vs. 321 non-members) applying quasi-experimental / econometric treatment-effect estimators (FIML Endogenous Switching Probit with instrumental-variable exclusion restrictions, Propensity Score Matching, and Inverse Probability Weighting)
why_tool_chosen: Although data come from a single 2019 cross-sectional survey, the study explicitly frames WRUA membership (institutionalized under Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016) as a binary policy/institutional intervention evaluated against a non-member comparator group (n = 331 vs. n = 321) to estimate causal Average Treatment Effects on the Treated (ATT) and Untreated (ATU) via Endogenous Switching Probit (with IV exclusion restrictions), Propensity Score Matching (PSM), and Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized intervention/policy evaluations using IV/PSM/IPW comparator designs are appraised with ROBINS-I rather than the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist.
selection_bias: Serious risk: Cross-sectional prevalent-user design recruiting existing WRUA members (n = 331) and non-members (n = 321) in September–December 2019 long after intervention uptake, using disproportionate stratified sampling across eight sub-catchments of unknown population size without reported sampling weights, and drawing simple random samples from a WRUA list with unreported non-response rates.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: Exposure and outcomes were collected contemporaneously through unblinded face-to-face CAPI interviews; subjective poverty and water-perception items are susceptible to self-report bias, and the Water Poverty Index embeds both right-hand-side socioeconomic covariates (land ownership, title, formal education, non-farm occupation, credit access) and the selection instrument (Water conflict) directly inside the composite outcome index.
confounding: Serious risk: Cross-sectional comparison lacks pre-intervention baseline poverty or water-access data, conditions on potentially endogenous post-treatment covariates (e.g., improved crops, electricity, credit access, livestock/TLUs), and relies on questionable exclusion restrictions (MWS-River, MWS-Borehole, Water conflict) that are plausibly affected by CWDP/WRUA water provision and violate exclusion for water poverty (Water conflict enters the WPI directly in Table A2 and has Coef. = 0.80, SE = 0.18 in Table A1 Model 5; joint falsification tests were not re-estimated after dropping MWS-Piped water).
attrition: No information / Not assessable: Single-wave cross-sectional survey with no longitudinal follow-up; the paper reports n = 652 (331 WRUA members, 321 non-members) but provides no information on target sample size, household refusal/non-response rates, or item-level missing data in the regressions.
reporting_bias: Serious risk: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan exists; continuous outcomes analyzed in a 2020 companion paper on the same catchment are dichotomized here (including a sample-relative 40th percentile cut-off for water poverty); Table 7 reports a positive IPW ATT for subjective poverty (+0.091**, SE = 0.039) whereas the text claims a 9% reduction; and Table A1 omits significance stars on Water conflict (Coef. = 0.80, SE = 0.18, z = 4.44) in the water-poverty falsification model while claiming validity.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / Moderate concern: The study situates Water Resource Users Associations (WRUAs) within Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016, but operationalizes the legal/institutional exposure solely as a cross-sectional household binary indicator (WRUA member = 1 vs. 0) that conflates Community Water Development Project (CWDP) water-supply group membership with sub-catchment WRUA regulatory governance and omits membership duration, water-permit status, fee payment, and rule enforcement.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: All four poverty outcomes (annual consumption, annual income, Economic Ladder Question, and polychoric-PCA Water Poverty Index) rely on single-visit household self-reports without physical water-quality or meter verification; Equation (A1) omits the Resources component in text while Table A2 lists five components; socioeconomic confounders and the Water conflict instrument are built into the WPI; and water poverty is defined via an arbitrary sample-relative 40th percentile cut-off.
where_found: Study design, sampling, variable construction, and econometric identification were appraised from Section 1 (PDF pp. 3–5), Section 2.1–2.4 (PDF pp. 5–9), Section 3.1–3.3 (PDF pp. 9–17), Tables 1–7 (PDF pp. 7, 10–14, 17), and Appendix Tables A1–A2 (PDF p. 22).

study_design_identified: Repeated cross-sectional observational study (pooled multilevel linear regression across four cross-sectional waves of India's National Sample Survey [1993, 2002, 2008-09, 2012] and single-wave multilevel logistic regression [2012] at the slum settlement level)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes four independent repeated cross-sectional waves of National Sample Survey slum-settlement data using observational multivariable linear and logistic regressions without following individual slums longitudinally and without a quasi-experimental intervention/comparator design (no DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, or ITS; the authors explicitly state on p. 29 that the NSS does not follow the same slums longitudinally and is not designed to establish causality). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression studies without a quasi-experimental intervention structure map to the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.
selection_bias: Some concern. The study draws on four nationally representative NSS urban slum rounds (1993, 2002, 2008-09, 2012; n = 2,901 slums) that explicitly sample non-notified as well as notified slums, avoiding Census undercounting of unrecognized settlements (p. 5). Analytic restriction to the 10 states with >=10 sampled slums per wave is clearly justified and retains 83.1% of sampled slums (2,411/2,901) with <0.9% complete-case loss (2,390/2,411; p. 6). However, exact NSSO operational criteria for classifying unnotified settlements as slums across rounds are not detailed in the paper (estimated total slums drop sharply in 2012 in Table 2), and demolition/relocation of non-notified slums over time (p. 28) may induce compositional survivor bias across waves.
measurement_bias: Some / Moderate concern. Both legal status (notified vs. non-notified and years notified) and service/funding outcomes are measured at the aggregate slum settlement level describing the 'majority of residents' rather than individual households (pp. 5-6, 29-30), obscuring intra-slum heterogeneity. The manuscript also does not report how NSS enumerators verified notification duration or 2012 government scheme receipt (e.g., official municipal records vs. local informant recall).
confounding: High / Serious concern for causal inference (Some concern for associational inference). Multilevel and fixed-effects regressions adjust for state effects, survey wave, slum household count (linear and quadratic), land ownership, fringe vs. central location, surrounding land use, and community association presence (pp. 10-11, Tables 5 and A4). However, the repeated cross-sectional design cannot rule out reverse causation (less-deprived or politically organized slums securing notification, p. 29; or prior improvement aid reducing 2012 BSDS in Regression 2, pp. 11-12) or unmeasured household- and city-level confounders (migrant recency, household income/wealth, caste, municipal fiscal capacity).
attrition: Low concern (longitudinal attrition not applicable; minimal cross-sectional item missingness). Because the NSS waves are independent cross-sections rather than a panel following the same slums over time (p. 29), longitudinal attrition does not apply; within the 10-state sample, complete-case restriction excluded only 21 of 2,411 slums (0.87%, leaving n = 2,390; p. 6).
reporting_bias: Low to Some concern. No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported (standard for secondary observational NSS analyses), leaving discretionary choices such as BSDS category cutpoints (<=30, 31-60, >60 in Regression 2; p. 12) unverified against prior specification. However, transparency is strong: the authors report minor NSSO replication discrepancies (p. 6), present individual component trends alongside composite scores (Table 3), and provide four full sensitivity models in Appendix Tables A1-A4.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality. Legal exposure captures formal government recognition ('notified' vs. 'non-notified' slum status) and notification duration ('years notified', modeled with linear and quadratic terms as well as a binary indicator in Table A1), complemented by public/central/private land-jurisdiction categories (pp. 10-12, 28). Key limitations are community-level homogeneity assumptions (masking household-level cutoff-date tenure rules in cities such as Mumbai, pp. 29-30), pooling heterogeneous state notification regimes without statutory disaggregation, and unreported NSS field verification procedures for years notified.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality. Basic water and sanitation services are operationalized using concrete NSSO settlement-level infrastructure indicators—drinking water source (tap, tubewell/handpump, well/other), latrine type (septic/flush/pour-flush, service/pit/public, none), underground sewer, covered/open drainage, monsoon waterlogging, and municipal solid waste collection (Table 1, p. 7)—reported separately (Table 3, p. 15) and combined into the Basic Services Deprivation Score (BSDS), whose weighting is validated across expert weights, polychoric factor analysis (Table A2), and NFHS-3 infant-mortality regression weights (Table A3). Limitations include majority-resident settlement coding without household coverage rates, water quality/continuity, or latrine-sharing metrics, and unverified informant reporting for 2012 JNNURM/RAY aid.
where_found: Methods and sample construction on PDF Pages 5-12 (Section 2, Table 1); descriptive and multivariable results on PDF Pages 12-25 (Section 3, Tables 2-6, Figures 1-3); methodological limitations (non-longitudinal cross-sectional design, reverse causation, unmeasured confounding, settlement-level ecological aggregation) on PDF Pages 29-30 (Section 4(iv)); sensitivity models on PDF Pages 37-41 (Appendix Tables A1-A4).

study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental longitudinal difference-in-differences combined with baseline propensity score matching (PSM-DiD) across harmonized decennial census tracts (1991, 2000, 2010)
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a non-randomized municipal legal/zoning intervention (implementation of Social Interest Special Zones, ZEIS) using a comparative quasi-experimental panel difference-in-differences design matched via baseline propensity score matching (PSM-DiD) across treated and untreated census tracts in Recife (1991, 2000 and 2010). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the designated instrument for non-randomized policy/intervention evaluations with a genuine comparator group.
selection_bias: Moderate risk: The authors appropriately exclude 381 prevalent ZEIS tracts treated between 1983 and 1991 (due to incompatible 1980 tract data), but restrict the primary treated sample from 132 post-1991 ZEIS tracts to the 19 tracts (18 in dynamic models) with >90% territorial ZEIS coverage matched to 54 PSM control tracts estimated on the >50% coverage group; robustness checks across 50%-100% cutoffs and 84 slum control tracts confirm stability, though household compositional sorting across tracts over 1991-2010 cannot be excluded.
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate risk: Both legal exposure (municipal PLHIS records and GIS shapefiles) and housing/utility outcomes (IBGE Demographic Censuses for 1991, 2000 and 2010) derive from standardized official sources independent of the evaluation, preventing differential observer bias, but spatial harmonization of census tracts creates partial-overlap boundary mismatch for ZEIS exposure and outcomes rely on household self-reports to census enumerators.
confounding: Serious risk: ZEIS designation was non-random and required municipal legislation and household mapping resources; only one pre-intervention census wave (1991) is available so pre-treatment parallel trends cannot be empirically tested; unobserved time-varying confounders (such as community political mobilization or concurrent localized public investments) and compositional residential sorting across decennial censuses cannot be ruled out; and regressions condition on time-varying post-treatment tract covariates (density, literacy, marital status and, in Table 6, income).
attrition: Low risk (at census-tract unit of analysis): Universal decennial IBGE Demographic Census tabulations yield a complete balanced panel across 1991, 2000 and 2010 in all primary specifications (73 tracts / 219 observations in Table 2; 72 tracts / 216 observations in Tables 3 and 6; 102 tracts / 306 observations in Table 4), although household-level in- and out-migration within tracts over the 19-year window is unobserved and Table 5 exhibits a minor unexplained discrepancy between treated tract counts across columns (18 vs 19).
reporting_bias: No information (no pre-analysis plan): No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan exists to verify pre-specification of the five housing quality outcomes, PSM covariates or the >90% spatial overlap baseline threshold, although the authors transparently report null findings (bathrooms per household and garbage collection) and extensive sensitivity checks across 50% to 100% ZEIS area cutoffs and alternative control groups.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong: The study accurately cites the municipal statutory framework (Recife Laws 14,511/1983, 14,947/1987 PREZEIS, 16,113/1995, 16,176/1996 and Master Plan Law 02/2021) and Federal Law 10,257/2001, and geocodes official municipal PLHIS implementation dates and GIS shapefiles onto census tracts; however, exposure measures statutory spatial demarcation share rather than verified parcel-level tenure regularization (usucapiao or CDRU) or actual PREZEIS infrastructure disbursements.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate: Access to piped water via the general public network and access to sewage collection via the general public network (alongside homeownership, bathrooms per household and garbage collection) are measured consistently across 1991, 2000 and 2010 using universal IBGE Demographic Census tract data; limitations include reliance on household self-reports without physical service-quality verification (such as continuity, potability or wastewater treatment), spatial boundary harmonization across 962 to 1,854 census tracts and a minor wording slip in Table 1's note describing utility shares as percentages of homeowners rather than households.
where_found: Institutional and statutory context in Section 2 (PDF pp. 5-10); econometric DiD specifications and identification assumptions in Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 10-13); PLHIS/shapefile exposure geocoding, IBGE Demographic Census harmonization (1991, 2000, 2010), sample restrictions and PSM baseline balance in Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 13-19, Table 1, Figures 2-4); main pooled and dynamic DiD results in Section 4 (PDF pp. 20-23, Tables 2-3); robustness checks for slum controls, 50%-100% ZEIS coverage shares, spatial spillovers and household income controls in Section 5 (PDF pp. 23-30, Tables 4-6, Figures 5-7).

study_design_identified: Non-randomized longitudinal/panel econometric policy evaluation using spatial econometrics (lagged-covariate OLS and spatial autoregressive/error MLE with urban-area fixed effects) and instrumental variables (2SLS and LIML) across Brazilian Minimum Comparable Areas (1970-2000)
why_tool_chosen: The study is a quantitative non-randomized evaluation of decentralized municipal exclusionary policy (under-providing public central water connections to small informal-sector housing under pre-1988 institutional rules) across 351-447 Brazilian localities (MCAs) in 55-123 urban areas over 1970-2000, employing urban-area fixed effects, spatial autoregressive/error maximum likelihood, and 2SLS/LIML instrumental-variables panel growth regressions with explicit counterfactual comparisons. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel econometric and IV policy evaluations map directly to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Moderate concern. Harmonizing split/merged municipalities into 447 Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs) across 123 urban areas avoids endogenous municipal boundary selection, but analytic samples condition on reaching >=50% urbanization in the base census year (351 MCAs in 55 multi-locality urban areas), drop localities with <10 surveyed small houses, and restrict non-linear strategic interaction models to 23 urban areas containing exactly 2 or 3 localities.
measurement_bias: Serious concern for policy exposure; moderate concern for outcomes. Intentional municipal exclusionary policy in the 1980s is not directly observed, but proxied by the share of small houses (defined as 1-2 rooms in 1980 vs. 1-3 rooms in 1991/2000) connected to a central public water network, conflating deliberate exclusion with technical/fiscal capacity backlogs and capturing non-migrant and formal small dwellings alongside informal migrant housing. Outcomes (water/full-service shares and 1991-2000 urban household growth) rely on standardized IBGE Census data but face household reporting error and shifting urban/rural classifications within suburban MCAs.
confounding: Serious concern. In Section 4 strategic servicing regressions, instruments for rival localities' policies (W'b) were unacceptably weak, leaving lagged-covariate OLS and spatial MLE vulnerable to unobserved 1980s local growth/backlog shocks and sensitive to spatial weight specification. In Section 5 growth regressions, urban-area fixed effects and 2SLS/LIML instruments (porous geology interacted with insolation plus 1970 census variables) address reverse causality from capacity backlogs, but geological/insolation instruments may directly affect contemporary private water supply or land costs, 1970 historical instruments rely on untestable serial-independence assumptions, and multivariate first-stage strength is modest (partial F ~ 13; 2SLS p < 0.10).
attrition: Low-to-moderate concern. Decennial IBGE Population Censuses cover the universe of Brazilian municipalities, and boundary splits/recombinations from 1970 to 2000 are harmonized into constant-boundary Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs), preventing panel unit attrition; however, item missingness rates are not reported and appended tables (PDF pp. 39-46, 48, 50) did not extract as text to verify exact estimation N across specifications.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan or protocol exists). As an observational 2008 NBER working paper, there is no pre-registered protocol. While the authors transparently report OLS alongside 2SLS/LIML, weak-instrument diagnostics, and counterfactual checks (1991 large houses and 2000 small houses), they select spatial weight matrices and instrument sets partly on specification tests and summarize multiple sensitivity regressions in prose as 'not reported' or 'not shown'.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate. The paper provides substantive institutional context on Brazil's 1979 national 125 m2 minimum lot-size law, pre-1988 illegality of municipal infrastructure provision in informal favelas and loteamentos, and post-1988 constitutional democratization/slum-upgrading reforms, plus descriptive data from 1999/2005 IBGE municipal zoning surveys. However, primary statutory citations and municipal enactment dates are absent, and core econometric models operationalize exclusionary policy indirectly via census water-connection rates for small houses rather than coded municipal laws or administrative service-denial rules.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-strong. Central piped water connections, full service (electricity, central water, central sewerage), and decennial household and educational growth are measured using nationally standardized IBGE Population Census microdata (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000) across harmonized MCAs, supplemented by 1980 district-fixed-effects rent hedonics in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. Limitations include household self-reporting of central connections and land title, shifting room-count definitions across census waves, urban reclassification within suburban MCAs, and absence of service continuity or water quality metrics.

study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (30 villages randomized 1:1 to targeted 50% sanitation subsidy vs. retail-price control, stratified by commune climate vulnerability; n = 2,821 unique household sales presentations) with ancillary qualitative stakeholder interviews (n = 13) and pilot cost-effectiveness analysis
why_tool_chosen: The study's core empirical causal design is a cluster-randomized controlled trial in which 30 rural Cambodian villages (clusters) were randomized 1:1 via Stata's randtreat function to receive targeted 50% sanitation subsidies or retail-price sales pitches, evaluating household- and village-level latrine sales conversion (pp. 2, 4–5). Although the authors also conducted 13 qualitative stakeholder interviews and a cost-scaling exercise to contextualize implementation and market distortion (pp. 4, 6–8), the paper frames its primary design as a clustered RCT, presents no standalone qualitative themes table or verbatim interview quotes in Results, and exhibits textbook post-randomization within-cluster participant recruitment issues that only the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trials variant (Domain D1b) is specifically designed to evaluate.
selection_bias: High risk: Although cluster allocation across the 30 villages was computer-randomized and stratified (p. 4), households were identified and approached after randomization by unblinded sales agents assisted by unblinded village authorities, restricted to households without a toilet where a decisionmaker was home (p. 4). Village authorities in treatment clusters were substantially more supportive in identifying poor households, producing a statistically significant imbalance in subsidy eligibility (51–52% in treatment vs. 45% in control, p = 0.00) driven by a 5 percentage point higher share of IDPoor households in treatment areas (p = 0.00), which the authors explicitly recognize as selection bias (pp. 6–7, 9).
measurement_bias: Some concerns / Moderate risk: Sales agents collecting eligibility and sales-order data were unblinded to cluster assignment and received sales commissions (pp. 4, 9). Household climate vulnerability was measured via a single subjective self-reported 1-year shock question vulnerable to differential interpretation or strategic reporting (p. 9), and independent M&E verification re-assessments covered approximately 10% of purchasing households only, excluding non-purchasing households (p. 4).
confounding: Low-to-moderate concern: Computer-generated village-level randomization across 30 clusters stratified by commune climate vulnerability status, supported by baseline cluster balance checks and village-clustered regressions controlling for climate vulnerability (pp. 4–5), protects village-level intent-to-treat estimates against baseline cluster confounding. However, post-randomization differential recruitment of IDPoor/eligible households within treatment villages (pp. 6–7, 9) introduces within-cluster selection/confounding risk for household-level comparisons, and comparisons between eligible and ineligible subgroups are non-randomized.
attrition: Some concerns / Moderate risk: Actual post-order latrine installation and customer cancellation rates were completely unmeasured because follow-up ended at the conclusion of the 7.5-month sales period; the authors note that 10–20% of orders are typically cancelled prior to installation (pp. 8–9), which could plausibly differ between subsidized and unsubsidized buyers. In addition, 1,598 repeat-visit records (including 36 sales) were excluded post hoc from the analytic dataset (p. 4, Footnote 17), and household non-contact/refusal denominators during village canvassing were not reported.
reporting_bias: Some concerns: No trial registration or pre-analysis plan is reported anywhere in the article. Main-text statistical reporting is incomplete—Table 1 presents marginal probabilities and p-values ('0.00') without sample sizes, standard errors, or confidence intervals, while balance checks and village-level regression tables are deferred to Supporting Information (pp. 4, 6). Post-hoc dropping of 1,598 duplicate visits (p. 4, Footnote 17) and minor internal numerical discrepancies across pages (treatment eligibility reported as 51% on p. 6 vs. 'close to 52%' on p. 7; subsidized repeat-visit buyers reported as 26 [1%] on p. 7 vs. 29 [2%] on p. 9) raise additional reporting concerns.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate concern: The subsidy targeting rule integrates two official Cambodian administrative classifications—the government IDPoor proxy-means poverty registry and commune-level Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) scores from the National Council for Sustainable Development—with the country-validated 10-item Cambodia Poverty Probability Index (PPI) and a fixed 50% price discount (pp. 2–4). outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (Some concerns): Although framed around access to climate-resilient sanitation, the study measured only point-of-pitch latrine purchase orders ('sales closing rate') rather than verified latrine delivery, physical installation, structural flood resilience, or household toilet use, explicitly omitting an estimated 10–20% order cancellation rate (pp. 8–9).

study_design_identified: Two-period microeconomic game-theoretic model coupled with a non-randomized comparative longitudinal panel econometric study (unbalanced panel, 2002–2021, Pooled OLS, Fixed Effects, and Random Effects, N = 983 regression observations)
why_tool_chosen: While Section 3 develops a formal two-period microeconomic model, Section 4 conducts an empirical comparative longitudinal panel evaluation (2002–2021) using Pooled OLS, Fixed Effects, and Random Effects to estimate the effect of municipal and state election years (vs. non-election years) and regulatory features on real sanitation tariff adjustments across Brazilian municipalities. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation of an institutional/political exposure with an explicit comparator maps to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Serious risk: Inclusion in the unbalanced panel required being regulated by one of the 88 ANA-recognized subnational agencies with online normative resolutions and having enacted at least one tariff adjustment between 2002 and 2021 (starting from the oldest located adjustment). As the authors explicitly note (PDF p. 14, p. 137), municipalities that enacted zero tariff adjustments over the entire study period—potentially those subject to the highest political interference—are completely excluded from the sample, inducing sample selection directly related to the regulatory outcome.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: When online normative resolutions had gaps exceeding one year and regulatory agencies did not reply to inquiries, nominal tariff adjustments were assumed to be 0% (PDF p. 10, p. 133), conflating missing administrative records with real tariff erosion once deflated by IPCA. Additionally, the text misstates the municipal election dummy definition (PDF p. 12, p. 135), Table 1 prints an impossible negative maximum (-0,661) for nominal adjustments (PDF p. 11, p. 134), Table 3 duplicates the eleicoes_municipais row label (PDF p. 13, p. 136), and the Hausman test p-value (0.003) is misinterpreted in the prose as failing to reject the null hypothesis (PDF p. 13, p. 136).
confounding: Serious risk: Municipal and state elections in Brazil occur on fixed nationwide 4-year schedules across all municipalities simultaneously, yet the panel regressions omit general calendar-year fixed effects (controlling only for a 2020 COVID-19 dummy, post-July 2020 Novo Marco dummy, municipal GDP, population, water/sewage coverage, ordinary contract revisions, utility ownership, and agency jurisdiction). Nationwide macroeconomic or IPCA inflation shocks in specific calendar years remain confounded with election years, and contemporaneous water/sewage coverage is included as a regressor despite theoretical endogeneity.
attrition: Serious risk: The dataset is an unbalanced panel (N = 1,142 total observations; N = 983 in Table 3 regressions, losing ~14% of observations due to missing SNIS sewage coverage data), post-entry tariff resolutions could not be located for all subsequent years, and multi-year gaps where contacted regulatory agencies did not respond were imputed as 0% nominal tariff adjustments without sensitivity checks (PDF pp. 10-13, pp. 133-136).
reporting_bias: No information on pre-specification, with incomplete reporting Concerns: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan exists. Although Pooled OLS, Fixed Effects, and Random Effects estimates are shown together in Table 3 (PDF p. 13, p. 136), coefficient estimates for the full vector of control variables (municipal GDP, population, contract revisions, Novo Marco dummy, 2020 pandemic dummy, state ownership, agency jurisdiction) are omitted from Table 3, one election regressor is mislabeled, and empirical tests of actual system expansion are absent despite SNIS coverage panel data being collected.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate with notable limitations: The authors compiled primary administrative tariff resolutions from 88 ANA-recognized subnational regulatory agencies (46 municipal, 26 state, 16 intermunicipal), coded ordinary contract equilibrium revisions (Revisão), distinguished municipal titularidade and agency jurisdiction, and included an indicator for the July 2020 Novo Marco do Saneamento (PDF pp. 10-14, pp. 133-137). However, statutory precision is limited, exact intra-year tariff adjustment dates relative to October elections are not distinguished, text descriptions contain coding typos (PDF p. 12, p. 135), and unconfirmed multi-year gaps in agency resolutions were assumed to represent 0% adjustments.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: Although the study's title and theoretical model focus on social welfare and sanitation network expansion, no physical water/sewage access, service quality, or welfare outcome is evaluated as a dependent variable in Section 4 (SNIS water and sewage coverage ratios AG001 and ES001 are used only as right-hand-side controls). The sole empirical dependent variable is an intermediate regulatory pricing measure (real tariff variation, Variação_real), which is vulnerable to misclassification from imputing 0% nominal changes whenever contacted agencies failed to respond about missing resolutions.

study_design_identified: Observational longitudinal panel (cohort) study of 290 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2008 to 2014 using two-way fixed-effects regressions, 1- to 3-year lagged models, and 7-year change regressions
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study tracks a longitudinal panel (cohort) of 290 Chinese prefecture-level cities across seven annual waves (2008-2014), estimating within-city associations over time via two-way fixed-effects models, 1- to 3-year lagged exposure models, and 2008-2014 change models. ROBINS-I was not chosen because the study does not evaluate a discrete policy intervention or comparator arm—in fact, the authors explicitly restricted the sample to 2008-2014 to exclude the 2014 State Council hukou reform and characterize their design as examining observational correlations with a continuous demographic share (% temporary residents). JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional was not chosen because the primary design is longitudinal city-year panel follow-up rather than a single cross-section. JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies therefore best matches this observational longitudinal panel design.
selection_bias: Moderate concern: Sampling covers nearly the universe of China's prefecture-level cities (290 cities from 2008 to 2014) from national administrative yearbooks (PDF p. 5), avoiding ad hoc case selection. However, unaddressed exclusion of 7-14 cities and 13%-22% of city-years due to missing yearbook data (Tables 2-3, PDF pp. 8-9) and reliance on public-security-registered >1-year temporary residents (excluding unregistered migrants) introduce potential selection/coverage bias.
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Exposure and outcomes come from standardized national yearbooks (PDF pp. 5-7), avoiding recall bias, but suffer from proxy and scaling biases: (1) temporary resident counts include only migrants residing >1 year who registered with public security authorities, omitting unregistered and short-term (<1 year) rural migrants and conflating all non-local temporary residents with rural mingong (PDF p. 6); (2) city-wide infrastructure totals cannot capture intra-city spatial access for migrant neighborhoods (PDF pp. 6, 11); and (3) total urban population (permanent + temporary) sits in the denominator of both the focal exposure (% temporary residents) and all per-capita outcomes (Table 1 Note 1, PDF p. 7), creating mechanical denominator dilution during rapid migrant inflows.
confounding: Moderate concern: Two-way fixed effects (city and year fixed effects) control for time-invariant municipal characteristics and common national shocks, alongside five time-varying socioeconomic/demographic covariates (GRP per capita, municipal spending per capita, high school/college enrollment proxy, registered unemployment rate, and population density) and restriction to pre-2014 to avoid the 2014 hukou reform (PDF pp. 5, 7-9). However, time-varying unobserved confounders (e.g., rapid industrialization or land-finance shifts driving both migrant inflows and per-capita infrastructure lag) remain possible, adult education is proxied by age 15-22 school/college enrollment (Note 4, PDF p. 12), and 3-year lagged estimates are null (PDF p. 10).
attrition: Moderate concern: A balanced 7-year panel of 290 cities (2008-2014) equals 2,030 city-years, yet estimation samples drop to 1,769 (283 cities) for green space, 1,730-1,737 (282-283 cities) for wastewater, and 1,577-1,589 (276 cities; 22.3% missing city-years and 14 omitted cities) for solid waste (Tables 2-3, PDF pp. 8-9). Reasons for missing cities/years are not explained and listwise deletion is used without sensitivity or imputation checks.
reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern (no preregistration reported): No pre-analysis plan or protocol is mentioned (Can't tell for formal pre-specification), but reporting across tested outcomes and sensitivity analyses is transparent, including prominent reporting of null results for public green space (Model 1, Table 3, PDF p. 9) and null 3-year lag specifications referenced in supplemental Tables A1-A5 (PDF p. 10).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: While China's hukou household registration system is discussed conceptually in detail (PDF pp. 4-5), the empirical analysis does not directly code or measure city-level or temporal variation in hukou legal rules, conversion quotas, or administrative entitlements. Instead, hukou-based institutional exclusion is proxied solely by the demographic percentage of public-security-registered >1-year temporary residents in each city (PDF p. 6).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Wastewater treatment capacity (10,000 m3/day per 10,000 persons), annual wastewater volume treated (10,000 m3 per 10,000 persons), solid waste treatment capacity (tons/day per 10,000 persons), annual solid waste treated (10,000 tons per 10,000 persons), and public green space (ha per 10,000 persons) come from official China Urban Construction Statistical Yearbooks (Table 1, PDF pp. 6-7). However, prefecture-level per-capita facility metrics cannot measure household sewer connectivity, actual service delivery to migrant enclaves, or treatment quality (PDF pp. 6, 11).

study_design_identified: Longitudinal municipal panel econometric policy evaluation (3 four-year mayoral terms, 2008-2019) using the Hausman-Taylor internal-instrumental-variables panel estimator
why_tool_chosen: S385 is a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel econometric evaluation estimating causal effects of fiscal, political, and administrative decentralization policies across Colombian municipalities over 2008-2019 using the Hausman-Taylor panel instrumental-variables estimator. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel and IV policy evaluations with continuous/categorical exposures across subnational jurisdictions map directly to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Moderate risk: All 1,103 Colombian municipalities delimited via digital elevation models were included in the target frame at the 2008 onset of the Law 1176/2007 SGP-APSB transfer regime, but entry into the analytic panel required reporting in SSPD's REC (which covers formal conventional providers rather than informal/community rural systems) and evaluates prevalent municipal decentralization structures established in the 1990s rather than new initiators.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: Fiscal and electoral indicators come from standardized administrative registries (DNP/CEDE, CGR, RNEC), but the administrative decentralization exposure (MDM) was only available starting in 2016 and was averaged over 2016-2019 and imputed backward across 2008-2015 as time-invariant (pp. 16-17, 23), introducing backward measurement error and post-outcome contamination; SSPD-REC outcome records also exclude non-conventional/community rural water systems (Footnote 4, p. 10).
confounding: Serious risk: Causal identification relies on internal Hausman-Taylor instruments whose exogeneity classifications were modified post hoc through iterative specification searches—reclassifying 2016-2019 administrative performance (MDM) and homicide rates as strictly exogenous instruments (pp. 18-19)—while omitting direct central-government municipal spending (Footnote 3, p. 9), Departmental Water Plans (PDA), private vs. public/community utility structure under Law 142, and common period shocks; Sargan-Hansen overidentification tests also fail in total coverage models (Tables 6-7, cols. 1 and 4).
attrition: Serious risk: From a national frame of 1,103 delimited municipalities (3,309 potential municipality-period observations across three mayoral terms; 2,878 coverage observations in Table A1), estimation samples drop without missing-data adjustment or sensitivity testing to 767-893 municipalities (1,631-2,188 observations in Tables 6-7), losing ~30% of all municipalities in rural sewerage regressions and ~38% of large/medium municipalities (dropping from 61 in Table 4 to 37-38 in Tables 6-7).
reporting_bias: Serious risk: No pre-analysis plan or protocol was registered, and the author explicitly describes multi-round specification searches ('aprendizaje estadístico', pp. 16, 18-19) across combinations of fiscal, political, and control variables—retaining variables (e.g., turnout only in rural sewerage; population density in Table 6 vs. rurality index in Table 7) and reclassifying endogenous/exogenous status based on statistical significance, sign stability, and passing post-estimation tests—while omitting fixed-effects and random-effects estimates (Footnote 9, p. 19).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: The national decentralization and water-sector legal framework (1991 Constitution, Laws 60/1993, 142/1994, 617/2000, and 1176/2007 SGP-APSB earmark and tariff-subsidy rules) is accurately described and fiscal transfers/revenues are measured in real per-capita terms from official DNP/CGR accounts, but municipal administrative capacity (MDM) is back-imputed from 2016-2019 onto 2008-2015 and municipal provider legal forms (ESP, EICE, community aqueducts, PDA membership) are not operationalized in the regressions.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Urban, rural, and total municipal aqueduct and sewerage coverage rates are drawn from official SSPD-REC administrative filings across 2008-2019 and log-normalized for boundedness (p. 14), but REC only counts residential connections served by formal conventional providers—systematically excluding ~25,500 community-managed/alternative rural providers (Footnote 4, p. 10; p. 25)—and captures nominal connection coverage rather than potability, continuity, or wastewater treatment quality.

study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional observational household survey study (multi-country binary probit and ordered probit regression analysis using Afrobarometer Round 7 data)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes cross-sectional observational household survey data from Round 7 of the Afrobarometer (2016-2018) to estimate statistical associations between regional utilities bribery incidence and self-reported water access using probit and ordered probit regressions, without any discrete policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental identification strategy (and explicitly disclaims causal inference). Therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
selection_bias: Some concern: The study uses Afrobarometer Round 7 (2016-2018) representative household surveys across 34 African countries employing Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) and GPS tracking to enforce random-walk respondent selection. However, the main text does not explicitly state individual respondent eligibility criteria, country selection criteria, survey response rates, or an explicit participant flow diagram, and coding non-seekers of utility services as zero in the bribery variable mixes service demand/contact into the exposure denominator.
measurement_bias: High concern: Both exposure and outcomes are derived from same-source household survey self-reports (plus subjective enumerator observation of area piped infrastructure) without independent objective verification. The bribery measure conflates water, sanitation, and electric utilities, conflates non-applicants with bribe-free users, is vulnerable to social desirability/reporting bias, and fails to replicate in Afrobarometer Rounds 5 and 6 (showing a null association in Round 5 and a positive association in Round 6 and pooled Rounds 5-7, which the authors attribute to pre-CAPI interviewer walk-pattern bias).
confounding: High concern for causal inference / Some concern for descriptive association: Models adjust for individual utilities bribery, enumerator-assessed area piped water infrastructure, household lived poverty index, urban/rural status, respondent gender, regional non-utilities corruption, and country fixed effects, and authors explicitly disclaim causal claims. Nevertheless, the cross-sectional design leaves substantial potential for reverse causality/simultaneity (water scarcity inducing bribery) and unmeasured subnational confounding (regional economic output, local fiscal capacity, climate/aridity, and utility-specific institutional governance).
attrition: Not applicable / Low concern: As a single-wave cross-sectional household survey (Afrobarometer Round 7), longitudinal panel attrition does not apply. Item-level missingness across regression specifications is minimal (<1%, ranging from N = 44,887 in unadjusted individual-bribe-omitted models to N = 44,778 in full models and N = 44,546 for the Homesource models), although household survey non-response rates are not reported in the article.
reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern (No information on pre-registration): No pre-analysis plan or protocol registration is reported. However, within-paper reporting transparency is strong: the authors report binary probit, full 5-category ordered probit, mixed-effects, PSU-level, leave-one-out regional corruption, and non-utilities corruption specifications, and candidly report null and opposite-signed estimates from Afrobarometer Rounds 5 and 6.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (Some concern): The study does not measure formal de jure water law, regulatory institutions, or statutory rules; instead, it proxies de facto administrative corruption using household self-reports of paying bribes, gifts, or favors to government officials for utilities, averaged at the subnational region level. Construct specificity for water governance is weakened because the Afrobarometer question bundles water, sanitation, and electricity services together and codes respondents who never sought services identically to those who sought services without paying a bribe (zero).
outcome_measurement_quality: Some concern (Weak-to-adequate): Water access is measured via a standardized 12-month recall survey question on how often the family went without enough clean water for home use, collapsed in primary models into a coarse binary indicator (anything other than 'always' coded as 1, meaning respondents lacking water 'many times' are coded as having access, though full 5-category ordered probit models and an Appendix sensitivity recoding are also reported) alongside self-reported source location (inside house, inside compound, outside compound). No objective physical water quality testing, meter continuity data, or technical JMP source verification is used.
where_found: Study design, survey description, variable operationalization, probit/ordered probit model specification, confounder controls, and causal disclaimers are in Section 4 (Data and Methods, PDF Pages 7-9 / pp. 125-127) and Section 1 (Introduction, PDF Page 2 / p. 120). Main regressions, subgroup splits by piped infrastructure, ordered probit checks, Round 5/6 comparisons, and water source location models are in Section 5 (Results/Discussion, PDF Pages 9-13 / pp. 127-131) and Endnotes 4-6 (PDF Page 14 / p. 132), referencing online Supporting Information Tables A1-A6.

study_design_identified: Ecological municipality-level observational regression study (lagged cross-sectional / two-period observational regressions of 2005 municipal piped water coverage and 2000-2005 cumulative per capita federal transfers on 1999-2000 municipal characteristics, without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study estimates observational multivariable regressions (fractional logit GLM and OLS) across a single cross-section of Mexican municipalities (with 2000 baseline covariates, 2000-2005 cumulative transfers, and 2005 piped water coverage proportion). There is no discrete policy intervention or quasi-experimental counterfactual design (ruling out ROBINS-I), and municipalities are ecological units with continuous baseline coverage and continuous indigenous share rather than incident-free exposed/unexposed cohorts (making the JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional Studies checklist the best-fitting tool per review guidance for observational regressions without a quasi-experimental intervention structure).
selection_bias: Some concern: The study covers nearly the entire national universe of Mexican municipalities using INEGI census and administrative records, avoiding voluntary sampling bias, but criteria for excluding 82 to 112 of Mexico's 2,454 municipalities (likely due to missing administrative/economic census records or undefined log transformations of zero values) are not reported.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Demographic indigenous share (indigenous language speakers) and household piped water connections are measured uniformly from national INEGI censuses/surveys, but key explanatory/control variables rely on coarse proxies—specifically, cumulative federal transfers bundle non-water programmes (health, education) with infrastructure, and municipal income from the 1999 Economic Census omits agricultural and informal income prevalent in rural indigenous municipalities.
confounding: Moderate to serious concern (observational ecological design): Regressions adjust for baseline 2000 water coverage, population density, formal per capita income, international migration, presidential vote share (Model 2), state fixed effects, and a spatial lag, but lack quasi-experimental identification and remain vulnerable to unobserved municipal confounders (e.g. terrain ruggedness/hydrology, intra-municipal settlement dispersion, informal/agricultural income, local administrative capacity) and simultaneity between 2000-2005 transfers and 2005 water coverage.
attrition: Low to moderate concern (unexplained municipal sample attrition across linked datasets): Although based on national municipal censuses rather than individual longitudinal tracking, analytic sample size drops from 2,454 Mexican municipalities (2,434 in Table 1) to 2,372 in Model 1 (Table 3) and 2,342 in Models 2-3 (Tables 4-5), representing 3.3% to 4.6% missingness without explanation or sensitivity analysis.
reporting_bias: Some concern (Can't tell on pre-specification): No pre-analysis plan or protocol is reported, summary statistics for transformed regression variables and state dummy coefficients are omitted, and mediation models (Tables 3 and 5) are estimated on slightly different sample sizes (2,372 vs 2,342), although Note 11 transparently reports robustness to specifying the dependent variable as piped water coverage growth.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (accurate constitutional framing but coarse fiscal proxy): Municipal water service responsibility under Article 115 of the Mexican Constitution and federal fiscal decentralisation are accurately described, and intergovernmental transfers are measured from official INEGI Public Finances records (Aportaciones Federales, 2000-2005, in constant 2002 pesos), but the measure aggregates infrastructure, health, education, and other transfers rather than isolating water-specific statutory transfer funds or allocation formulas.
outcome_measurement_quality: Good for physical network coverage, limited for service quality: Measured consistently across municipalities using INEGI 2000 Population Census and 2005 Population Survey enumerations of households with a piped water network connection inside the dwelling, though census connection indicators do not capture water potability, continuity/intermittency, pressure, or affordability.
