study_design_identified: Non-randomized comparative policy evaluation using repeated cross-sectional household surveys (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005) and a difference-in-differences (DiD) probit regression model across four Bolivian cities, supplemented by secondary institutional/regulatory background
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical design is a quantitative non-randomized comparative evaluation of a policy intervention (water utility privatization in La Paz and El Alto vs. comparator utilities in Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Cochabamba) using repeated cross-sectional household microdata before and after reform and an explicit difference-in-differences (DiD) probit regression model (Sections 3-4, pp. 3-6; Section 6, p. 11). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized comparative intervention/policy evaluations (including DiD and controlled before-after designs) map directly to ROBINS-I. Although Section 2 and Section 7 discuss institutional and contractual context, those sections draw on secondary literature and regulatory reports rather than primary qualitative fieldwork, so MMAT does not apply.
selection_bias: Serious — While the study uses official INE household surveys across Bolivia's four largest cities, survey documentation did not specify the sampling design ('sampling method not specified', Note 13, p. 13; analyzed as simple random samples, p. 4), sample sizes dropped sharply in later waves (most acutely to n = 56 in El Alto in 2001; Table 2, p. 3), and the affordability analysis conditions on post-intervention utility connection ('connected households only', p. 11), which biases cross-period affordability estimates when poor households are disconnected (as occurred in Cochabamba between 2001 and 2005).
measurement_bias: Serious — Survey definitions of 'piped water' changed between the pre-privatization surveys (1992 and 1996, which specified piped water from the utility network inside the dwelling or yard) and the post-privatization surveys (2001 and 2005, which recorded generic 'piped water' without specifying inside dwelling/yard or utility vs. private network; Table 4, p. 4). Surveys also could not separate protected from unprotected wells/boreholes, and affordability relied on self-reported prior-month expenditure without water quantity consumed, confounding price changes with consumption adjustments and post-privatization metering/billing of previously free connections (pp. 5, 10; Note 21, p. 13).
confounding: Serious — Privatization was non-randomly adopted across only four cities (two treated: La Paz and El Alto; two comparators: Santa Cruz and Cochabamba). Pre-reform coverage trends (1992-1996) differed substantially across cities (Table 7, p. 7; Figure 4, p. 8) and were not controlled in the DiD regressions; household covariates were restricted to log per-capita income (potentially endogenous; Note 17, p. 13) or only three basic dwelling variables due to cross-survey incompatibility (Note 18, p. 13); time-varying city-level economic/demographic shocks and differential population growth were unadjusted; and standard errors were not clustered at the city level (only 4 clusters).
attrition: Moderate — Because the study uses repeated cross-sectional household surveys rather than a longitudinal panel, individual panel attrition does not apply, and item-level missingness in the 1996/2001 and 1996/2005 probit regressions is low (<3%; Table 2 vs. Table 12). However, 1996 water expenditure data were completely unavailable, preventing any pre- vs. post-privatization affordability comparison (Section 3(c), p. 5), and survey sample sizes shrank markedly across waves (especially El Alto n = 56 in 2001; Table 2, p. 3).
reporting_bias: No information — No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol is mentioned. Although the authors report both short-run (1996-2001) and longer-run (1996-2005) DiD estimates, two covariate specifications (Table 12, p. 11), and sensitivity across Kakwani effort-appreciation parameters (e = 0.1, 0.5, 1), selective model specification (such as excluding the 1992 pre-reform wave from the econometric regression) cannot be ruled out in the absence of a registered protocol.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate — The legal, contractual, and regulatory architecture of Bolivia's water concessions (1906 Ley de Aguas, 1994 Ley 1600, 1997 Regulation of Concessions, Laws 2029/2066 creating SISAB, contractual expansion targets, tariff dollarization, elimination of communal standpipes, and the 2005 SISAB independent audit) is well documented in Section 2 (pp. 2-3) and Notes 3-9 (pp. 12-13). However, the quantitative DiD analysis operationalizes exposure as a coarse time-invariant city binary ('privatized' vs. 'non-privatized') that codes Cochabamba as non-privatized despite its 1999-2000 Aguas del Tunari privatization, 35% tariff hike, and 'water war' cancellation.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to Moderate — Household water access and monthly water expenditure are drawn from official national household surveys (INE), avoiding investigator-induced recall bias, but cross-wave questionnaire non-equivalence in water-source categories (Table 4, p. 4), lack of data on water quality, pressure, or continuity, absence of 1996 baseline expenditure data, and lack of volumetric water consumption substantially limit outcome measurement validity.
where_found: Institutional and legal context in Section 2 (pp. 2-3, Table 1) and Notes 3-11 (pp. 12-13); survey data sources, sample sizes, water-access definitions, and delivery/equity/affordability methods in Section 3 (pp. 3-5, Tables 2-4) and Notes 12-15 (p. 13); DiD probit specification and causal caveats in Section 4 (pp. 5-6) and Notes 16-18 (p. 13); descriptive delivery, equity, and affordability results in Section 5 (pp. 6-11, Tables 5-11, Figures 3-6) and Appendix A (p. 14); DiD regression results in Section 6 (p. 11, Table 12).

study_design_identified: Observational longitudinal panel study (unbalanced utility-level panel regression of 75 urban/peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries, 1996-2009 [1995-2012 data], modeling prospective 3-year changes in water coverage via pooled OLS, fixed effects, and random effects)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies
why_tool_chosen: The empirical analysis tracks a longitudinal panel of water utilities forward over 3-year intervals (t to t+3 across 1995-2012) to examine how a continuous baseline operational characteristic (O&M cost recovery ratio) predicts subsequent changes in water coverage, without a discrete policy/intervention assignment or quasi-experimental comparator structure (such as DiD, IV, RDD, ITS, or matched treated/untreated policy arms). Because it is longitudinal rather than cross-sectional, and observational/exposure-based rather than a non-randomized evaluation of an assigned intervention, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies is the most appropriate instrument.
selection_bias: High concern: Inclusion into the analytic sample required voluntary reporting and non-missing longitudinal fields in IBNET, reducing >200 utilities in 42 SSA countries to 75 utilities in 25 countries (PDF pp. 4-5), with nearly half of utilities drawn from just three countries (Nigeria = 18, Zambia = 10, South Africa = 8; Table 7, PDF p. 13), rural water schemes excluded by construction (except potential rural inclusion in 3 South African district municipalities tested in Model h5), and ~20 observations with O&M cost recovery >2.0 dropped in main models (Note 13, PDF p. 10). Aggregate sample means were checked against regional benchmarks in Table 3 (PDF p. 6), but utility-level selection bias remains substantial.
measurement_bias: High concern: Both the primary exposure (O&M cost recovery) and outcome (3-year change in water coverage) derive from utility self-reported IBNET benchmarking records affected by general quality problems, inconsistent utility ID numbers across years, and figure revisions between the March 2011 and May 2013 IBNET downloads requiring manual matching (PDF pp. 9-10, Note 17). Baseline water coverage exhibits out-of-range values up to 127% and 3-year coverage changes span -81 to +72 percentage points (SD = 18.28; Table 5, PDF p. 12), while O&M cost recovery is distorted by arrears/delayed payments (>2.0 in ~20 truncated observations; Note 13, PDF p. 10) and country-level controls combine 2001-05 averages (public spending) and 2008-2012 projections (ODA) divided by fixed 2005 GDP (Table 2, PDF p. 5).
confounding: High concern: Identification relies on lagging explanatory variables by 3 years (Eq. 1, PDF p. 4) and estimating pooled OLS, utility fixed-effects, and utility random-effects models without exogenous policy variation or quasi-experimental identification. Regressing the 3-year change (Y_{t+3} - Y_t) on initial coverage (Y_t) induces mechanical measurement-error mean-reversion and dynamic panel (Nickell) bias in short panels; the Hausman test rejects random-effects consistency (chi2 = 20.74, Table 4, PDF p. 7); public expenditure (2001-05 country average) and ODA/urbanization are measured only at the country level; and critical time-varying institutional confounders such as corruption, tariff structures, and existence of a regulator are omitted (PDF p. 9).
attrition: High concern: Out of more than 200 Sub-Saharan African utilities from 42 countries in IBNET, only 75 utilities from 25 countries (235 utility-year observations; 72 utilities and 225 observations in models including public expenditure) had complete data on the 3-year water coverage difference and covariates (PDF pp. 4-5, 9). Within the retained unbalanced panel spanning 1996-2009, 29 of 75 utilities contribute only 1 observation and 22 contribute only 2 observations (Table 7, PDF p. 13), and no imputation or inverse-probability weighting was applied.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan): No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported, and main specifications impose an ex post truncation of O&M cost recovery <= 2.0 (excluding ~20 observations; Note 13 on PDF p. 10 acknowledges that un-truncated linear models yielded negative coefficients). However, transparency is strengthened by reporting nine OLS, fixed-effects, and random-effects specifications in Table 4 (PDF p. 7), inner-fence random-effects Tobit outlier models in Appendix B (Table 8, PDF p. 13), and seven sample/covariate sensitivity models in Appendix C (Table 9, PDF p. 14), alongside a minor reversed significance-level footnote typo in Table 4.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Although the study motivates and interprets its findings around corporatization, performance contracts, donor loan covenants, and regulatory cost-recovery targets (e.g., NWASCO in Zambia), no statute, regulation, contract, or regulatory target is directly coded or measured in the empirical analysis. Instead, achieved accounting O&M cost recovery (operating revenues divided by operating and maintenance costs) is used as an indirect operational proxy, and the authors explicitly note that existence of a regulator had to be excluded due to unavailable data (PDF p. 9), with only a coarse 3-tier jurisdictional dummy (national, regional/state, municipal) added in Appendix C Model h4 (PDF pp. 13-14).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Water access is measured via utility-reported IBNET water coverage (population with direct service connection or within reach of a public water point as a percentage of nominal population under utility responsibility) and its 3-year difference (Table 2, PDF p. 5). The binary coverage metric omits water quality, hours/continuity of supply, affordability, and household connection versus standpost distinctions (PDF p. 4), and exhibits severe reporting error/volatility including maximum initial coverage of 127% and 3-year swings from -81 to +72 percentage points (Table 5, PDF p. 12).
where_found: Study design, data sources, variable definitions, and sample composition in Section 3 and Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 4-6) and Appendix A Tables 5-7 (PDF pp. 12-13); regression specifications and main estimates in Section 4 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 6-8); study limitations in Section 5 (PDF p. 9); data matching, sample truncation, and methodological caveats in Notes 8-26 (PDF pp. 10-11); outlier Tobit and covariate robustness checks in Appendices B-C and Tables 8-9 (PDF pp. 12-14).

study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal panel study (5-year balanced municipal panel, 2015-2019, N = 1,720 across 344 Brazilian municipalities directly providing WWS, estimated via two-way fixed-effects, random-effects, and Mundlak correlated random-effects regressions)
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a public governance arrangement/policy intervention—municipal participation in horizontal intermunicipal cooperation (public consortia) and cooperation duration—using longitudinal panel regression models (two-way fixed effects, random effects, and Mundlak correlated random effects) comparing participating vs. non-participating Brazilian municipalities directly providing WWS over 2015-2019. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel policy evaluations with a non-randomized comparator arm map directly to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Serious concern: Inclusion is restricted to a complete-case balanced panel of 344 municipalities representing only 23.4% of Brazilian municipalities that directly provide WWS (6.2% of all municipalities), likely selecting higher-capacity providers; moreover, 54 of 71 IMC municipalities entered cooperation before the 2015 baseline (mean IMCd = 6.92 years), introducing prevalent-user / survivorship bias when estimating duration effects because early-exiting consortia prior to 2015 are unobserved.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Exposure (MUNIC) and outcomes (SNIS) come from standardized national administrative surveys rather than researcher-collected subjective ratings, but SNIS utility indicators are self-reported by local providers, and improvements in metering or accounting under consortium maturation could systematically alter measured water loss ratios (QUA) and operational revenue/expense ratios (FIN).
confounding: Serious concern: Municipality and year fixed effects absorb time-invariant municipal heterogeneity and common macro shocks, but time-varying municipal confounders (local fiscal stress, electoral/managerial shifts, targeted state/federal infrastructure transfers) are unmeasured; only log population is retained (GDP per capita was dropped), and in a 5-year panel where 54 of 71 treated municipalities were already in IMC at baseline, cooperation duration (IMCd) is confounded with differential municipal time trends.
attrition: Serious concern (missing data / complete-case panel restriction): Requiring non-missing MUNIC and SNIS observations across all five years (2015-2019) excludes 76.6% of Brazilian municipalities that directly provide WWS, with no missing-data diagnostics, attrition comparisons, or reweighting.
reporting_bias: No information (unregistered observational study with minor specification-selection concern): No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is reported; preliminary regressions including GDP per capita and regional controls are mentioned as not altering substantive results (p. 4) without being tabulated, and several highlighted fixed-effects findings rely on 10% significance (p < 0.10), though FE, RE, and Mundlak CRE models are transparently reported side-by-side across all four outcomes (Tables 3-6).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / adequate administrative proxy: Participation in intermunicipal cooperation via public consortia (IMC binary indicator) and years of participation (IMCd) are drawn from IBGE's official MUNIC municipal survey (2015-2019), accurately capturing formal horizontal consortium membership, but treating public consortia as a uniform indicator without coding consortium legal bylaws, contractual scope, regulatory oversight, or operational vs. planning functions.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / standard sector indicators with proxy limitations: Financial balance (FIN, operational revenue to total service expense), water coverage (WC), and wastewater coverage (WWC) follow standard SNIS definitions, while service quality (QUA) relies solely on the inverted water-loss volume ratio ((produced - consumed)/produced), omitting potability, continuity/intermittency, and wastewater treatment quality, and remaining vulnerable to uncalibrated macrometering/micrometering in smaller municipalities.
where_found: Study design, data sources (IBGE MUNIC and SNIS, 2015-2019), variable definitions, and sample inclusion/attrition (344 of ~1,470 direct-provision municipalities; 23.4%) are reported in Abstract ([PDF Page 1 of 9]) and Section 3.1 & Tables 1-2 ([PDF Page 3-4 of 9]). Econometric specifications (two-way FE, RE, Mundlak CRE), identification limits (71 IMC participants, only 17 switchers), and clustered inference are detailed in Section 3.2 ([PDF Page 4-5 of 9]). Empirical estimates and causal caveats appear in Section 4 & Tables 3-6 ([PDF Page 5-7 of 9]), and study limitations (secondary data, 5-year window, proxy quality indicator) are discussed in Section 6 ([PDF Page 8 of 9]).

study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal municipal panel study using difference-in-differences (DiD) combined with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching (2000-2010 Census and 2000-2008 PNSB), informed by 36 auxiliary retrospective semi-structured telephone interviews for propensity-score covariate selection.
why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact design-matched instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study's primary empirical design is a non-randomized comparative evaluation of competing governance interventions (water user association vs. local government rural water supply systems) using longitudinal panel difference-in-differences combined with multinomial propensity-score kernel matching (Section 3, PDF p. 5). Although Section 4(b) (PDF pp. 6-7) and Appendix A.1 (PDF p. 15) report 36 semi-structured telephone interviews conducted in 2013-2014, these interviews play an auxiliary covariate-selection role for the propensity-score specification (explicitly described by the author on PDF p. 12 as "anecdotal evidence provided by sector experts in the interviews, which informed this study") rather than constituting a co-equal mixed-methods primary study, making ROBINS-I more appropriate and informative than MMAT.
selection_bias: Moderate risk / concern: The study draws on the national universe of Brazilian municipalities in the 2000/2010 Censuses and 2000/2008 PNSB, comparing municipalities with new WUA (n = 583) versus new local-government (n = 592) rural water systems (and n = 3,717 no-change municipalities in Table 12). Excluding municipalities that split boundaries between 2000 and 2008 (PDF p. 5) and restricting to complete covariates and matching support drops ~14.2% of project municipalities in Table 4 (1,008 of 1,175 municipalities), though a Nijman-Verbeek test for pre-2000 boundary splits shows no significant selection bias (Table 5 col. 7, PDF pp. 9-10).
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate risk (Moderate for exposure classification, Low for outcome measurement): Provider governance and piped-water outcomes come from independent national IBGE instruments (PNSB 2000/2008 and Demographic Census 2000/2010). However, exposure measurement exhibits moderate misclassification risk because municipalities with both new local-government and WUA rural systems (256 municipalities in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6) are pooled into +assoc (Note 9, PDF p. 13), exact project start dates within 2000-2008 are unknown, and projects started in 2009-2010 fall between the 2008 PNSB exposure wave and the 2010 Census outcome wave (PDF p. 4). Outcome measurement via national census enumeration is standardized and objective across groups.
confounding: Serious risk / concern: Municipality fixed effects (DiD) combined with multinomial probit kernel matching (Heckman et al., 1997, 1998; Lechner, 2001, 2002), an urban access placebo regression (Table 5 col. 2, PDF p. 9), and a 1990-2000 pre-trend check (Table 5 col. 6, PDF pp. 9-10) remove time-invariant heterogeneity and municipality-wide trends. However, two ROBINS-I confounding issues remain: (1) unobserved time-varying differences in external donor/state financial and technical support bundled with WUA umbrella models in Northeast Brazil (CENTRAL, KfW-funded SISAR, PROSAR, CAERN subsidies; PDF p. 3) alongside inability to separate municipal water/sanitation spending from health expenditure (Table 3 note, PDF p. 7); and (2) conditioning the preferred propensity-score specification (Table 10 cols. 7-9; Appendix A.4, PDF pp. 19-21) on concurrent/post-baseline changes during 2000-2008 and 2000-2010 (Change to regional main, Change to local main, Delta Pop dens, Delta Admin).
attrition: Moderate risk / concern: PNSB non-response is low (188/5,507 municipalities in 2000 and 133/5,564 in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6), but excluding boundary-splitting municipalities, missing covariates, and kernel-matching common support reduces the two-group project sample from 1,175 municipalities (Table 1, PDF p. 4) to an unbalanced panel of 1,899 observations across 1,008 municipalities in Table 4 cols. 1-3 and 955 complete municipal pairs in the bootstrapped difference test in col. 4 (~18.7% attrition from the 1,175 total; PDF p. 8). Pre-2000 municipal splits also restrict the 1990-2000 pre-trend check to 556 municipalities (865 observations; Table 5 col. 6, PDF p. 9), though a Nijman-Verbeek selection indicator (st1) finds no significant structural difference (PDF pp. 9-10).
reporting_bias: No information (no pre-analysis plan or protocol): No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan exists to verify whether the propensity-score covariate set, matching bandwidth/specification, or the six accountability channel interactions in Table 6 (PDF p. 11) were pre-specified. Transparency is aided by extensive robustness tables (Tables 4-5, Appendix Tables 10-12), though one sensitivity check mentioned in Note 9 (treating Main + loc + assoc as a separate unweighted category; PDF p. 13) is not tabulated.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality: Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-4) accurately situates municipal decentralization, CESB concessions, the 2007 national sanitation law's social-control councils (conselhos gestores), rural development councils, and WUA concession/umbrella arrangements (CENTRAL, SISAR, PROSAR), informed by 36 retrospective semi-structured telephone interviews in 2013-2014 (Section 4(b), PDF pp. 6-7; Appendix A.1, PDF p. 15). study_design_identified: Non-randomized post-intervention comparative cross-sectional study (controlled observational evaluation comparing two DMM intervention slums with an adjacent non-DMM control slum via kiosk customer-intercept surveys, structured kiosk observations, and microbiological water sampling)
why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I was selected because the study explicitly evaluates a municipal utility governance intervention—KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model (DMM) implemented in Nyalenda A and B—using an adjacent untreated settlement (Manyatta B) explicitly designated as a 'control' slum to identify impacts of DMM (PDF p. 4, Sections 1.3 and 2). JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies was ruled out because the study is structured as an explicit intervention-versus-control program evaluation rather than an associational cross-sectional survey without an intervention comparator. MMAT was ruled out because open-ended survey questions and kiosk observations were quantized into percentages and one-way ANOVAs without an independent qualitative analytical strand (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).
selection_bias: Serious risk of bias (community-group-managed kiosks [~5%] were excluded from the sampling frame; kiosk sample counts are inconsistent [90 stated vs 44+28+25 = 97 vs N = 103 in queue ANOVA]; and intercepting adult customers at operating utility kiosks post-intervention conditions on active kiosk patronage, excluding DMM households with private piped connections, households priced out to wells/vendors, and child water collectors)
measurement_bias: Moderate risk of bias (microbiological E. coli and total coliform testing used objective laboratory membrane filtration, and per-20L kiosk price is salient, but monthly household water expenditure, 6-month supply reliability satisfaction, and service complaints relied on retrospective self-reports collected by unblinded local student interviewers, and kiosk observations coincided with a day-two main-line outage in DMM slums)
confounding: Serious risk of bias (only two non-randomly targeted DMM slums, which also received external French donor capital investment and WSP technical assistance, are compared post-intervention to a single adjacent control slum via unadjusted one-way ANOVAs without pre-intervention baseline measurements, regression controls, or cluster-level adjustment)
attrition: No information / Can't tell (single-wave cross-sectional data collection in May-June 2013; complete item data for all 294 interviewed customers in price and expenditure ANOVAs [df = 2, 291] and 22 household water samples from every 13th respondent, but kiosk and customer refusal/non-response rates are not reported and kiosk sample totals are internally inconsistent: 90 stated vs 97 summed across strata vs 103 implied by F(2, 100))
reporting_bias: Serious risk of bias (no pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol; microbiological results for the 8 kiosk and 22 household samples are pooled rather than reported separately for DMM vs control slums despite water quality being a stated comparative outcome and basis for concluding DMM improved safe water access, and household water quantity consumed is listed as an evaluation dimension in Section 4 without comparative results)
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate institutional description (grounded in Kenya Water Act 2002, WASREB licensing, KIWASCO's bulk-supply master-operator vs direct-kiosk governance arrangements, and informal landlord-tenant lease restrictions, but operationalized strictly as a settlement-level binary indicator without coding formal DMM contracts, tariff schedules, or regulatory instruments)

study_design_identified: Quantitative longitudinal uncontrolled before-and-after (pre-post) policy evaluation across 53 municipalities comparing 5-year pre-update and 5-year post-update administrative windows via municipality-specific robust paired-samples t-tests
why_tool_chosen: The study empirically evaluates the longitudinal before-and-after impact of a legal/administrative policy intervention—municipal cadastral updating ('actualización catastral' governed by Ley 1450 de 2011 Art. 24)—on municipal fiscal extraction and water/sanitation outcomes across 53 Colombian municipalities using each municipality's 5-year pre-intervention window as the comparator for its 5-year post-intervention window. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a multi-unit quantitative non-randomized pre-post evaluation of a policy/administrative intervention maps directly to ROBINS-I (unlike JBI Cross-Sectional, as observations are longitudinal pre/post windows rather than a single cross-section, and unlike single-case narrative histories).
selection_bias: Moderate risk: The target universe covers the complete census of 53 municipalities in Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda, avoiding arbitrary convenience sampling at the study-entry stage. However, conditioning inclusion in the water/sewerage (n = 33) and IRCA (n = 42) sub-analyses on calendar-year overlap between municipal cadastral update dates (2006/2008 onward) and national platform data availability systematically excludes earlier-updating and data-poor municipalities.
measurement_bias: Serious risk: While data come from official national repositories (IGAC, DNP-OEC/TerriData/SICODIS, SSPD-SUI, INS-SIVICAP), severe measurement artifacts affect the outcomes: (1) 20 of 33 analyzed municipalities had anomalous outlier values in SUI water/sewerage subscriber reports (Footnote 3); (2) aqueduct and sewerage coverage were approximated via an author-constructed proxy dividing SUI subscribers by IGAC cadastral parcels, mechanically coupling the denominator to the cadastral update intervention itself (and yielding -Inf t-statistics and NaN effect sizes in Table 6); (3) IRCA changes reflect varying annual sanitary sampling frequency alongside water contamination; and (4) 2000–2020 monetary series (property tax and SGP transfers) have no reported inflation adjustment.
confounding: Critical risk: The design relies exclusively on municipality-by-municipality univariate paired t-tests comparing 5-year pre-update and 5-year post-update periods (trimmed means with df = 2 or 3) without a contemporaneous control group, panel fixed effects, inflation deflation, or covariate adjustment. Secular time trends, nominal price growth, urbanization dynamics, national transfer formulas (Ley 1176 de 2007; indigenous reserve allocations), and concurrent municipal fiscal strategies (tax statute reforms under Ley 1450 de 2011, arrears recovery drives, early-payment incentives) are completely confounded with cadastral updating.
attrition: High concern / Serious risk: Although all 53 municipalities are retained in the narrative property-tax totals, 1 municipality (Aranzazu) is dropped from SGP transfer analyses, 20 of 53 municipalities are absent from water and sewerage subscriber/coverage analyses (15 due to pre-2008 cadastral update timing relative to SUI data availability and 5—Marmato, Norcasia, Pensilvania, Pueblo Rico and Córdoba—due to missing SUI data, with several remaining municipalities truncated to 4-year windows), and 11 of 53 municipalities are excluded from IRCA water-quality analyses (Aranzazu plus 10 municipalities missing SIVICAP/IRCA observations). Missingness in municipal utility and sanitary reporting is plausibly correlated with local institutional capacity.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan): No pre-registration or protocol exists. While the author transparently reports null findings across outcomes and candidly discusses SUI outliers and confounding mechanisms, Tables 2, 3 and 4 truncate printed rows at 42 municipalities despite the text reporting analyses of 53 (Tables 2–3) and 52 (Table 4) municipalities, Table 7 prints 41 rows instead of the stated 42 (and omits a significance asterisk on Palestina at p = 0.042), and stated observation year ranges vary inconsistently across p. 103, p. 112 and p. 113. Conducting roughly 300 unadjusted municipality-level tests at alpha = 0.05 also inflates family-wise Type I error.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern: Cadastral update years are drawn from official IGAC (2020) administrative records anchored to the statutory 5-year update mandate (Ley 1450 de 2011, Art. 24), and statutory SGP rules (Constitución Arts. 356–357, Ley 715, Decreto 416 de 2007, Ley 1176 de 2007) are accurately cited. However, exposure operationalization treats cadastral updating as a binary municipal event despite asynchronous urban-only or rural-only updates in 6 municipalities (e.g., La Tebaida, Circasia, Montenegro, Génova, Pijao, Pueblo Rico), includes the update year itself inside Period 1 without verifying fiscal effective dates, and does not measure parallel municipal tax-code or collection reforms.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: Water and sewerage coverage were not taken from verified household access surveys or consistent official coverage series, but from an improvised proxy ratio of SUI subscribers to cadastral parcels (whose formula image on PDF p. 7 is not rendered in text and whose denominator shifts with cadastral updating), unable to disaggregate urban vs. rural service areas. SUI subscriber counts suffered from documented reporting outliers in 20 municipalities, and INS-SIVICAP IRCA water-quality scores suffered from inconsistent annual sample counts and missing municipal series.
where_found: Design, administrative data sources (IGAC, DNP-OEC/TerriData/SICODIS, SSPD-SUI, INS-SIVICAP), proxy coverage description, sample restrictions, and Walrus Robust Paired Samples T-Test procedures are reported in 'Metodología y Datos' on PDF pp. 6–7 (pp. 102–103). Municipality update cohorts and pre/post periods appear in 'Resultados' and Tabla 1 on PDF p. 8 (p. 104), with statistical test outputs in Tablas 2–7 and narrative interpretations on PDF pp. 9–16 (pp. 105–112). Co-interventions, SUI outliers (Footnote 3), IRCA sampling variability, and urban/rural disaggregation limitations are detailed in 'Resultados' (PDF pp. 11, 16; pp. 107, 112) and 'Conclusiones' (PDF p. 17; p. 113).

study_design_identified: Quantitative observational analytical cross-sectional study (descriptive horizontal/vertical inequality decompositions across repeated cross-sectional DHS household survey waves [1990-2013; 2003-2013 for infrastructure], combined with static cross-sectional OLS regressions across spatial LGA-ethnic state partitions and LGAs)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: S407 conducts descriptive inequality analysis across repeated cross-sectional DHS waves and tests historical/institutional hypotheses using static cross-sectional OLS regressions (Equation 3) on pooled multi-year DHS polygon means (N = 631 LGA-ethnic partitions) and single-wave 2013 DHS / 2012 Afrobarometer LGA means (N = 127-162). It employs no quasi-experimental intervention evaluation design (no DiD pre/post policy panel, IV, RDD, PSM, or ITS) and explicitly characterizes its regression findings as cross-sectional correlations (p. 342). Therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
selection_bias: Some concern: Although DHS household surveys are nationally representative within surveyed areas, restricting spatial regressions to the 685 of 1,415 LGA-ethnic partitions (61 of 117 Murdock ethnic groups; N = 631 complete cases in Tables 4-5) with georeferenced DHS clusters and Murdock scores, and to N = 127-162 units in the 2012 Afrobarometer regressions (Tables 6-7), introduces potential spatial selection bias. Additionally, the 1990 DHS wave omitted the Northcentral and Southsouth zones altogether (Note 13).
measurement_bias: Moderate to High concern: Precolonial centralization relies on Murdock's (1967) Ethnographic Atlas (compiled from 20th-century ethnographic accounts to approximate c. 1850 institutions) intersected spatially with modern LGAs (r ~ 0.70 with self-reported ethnicity). Crucially, elite noncompliance with the 1976 military reform is proxied by a 1952 >70% Muslim state dummy, and local government quality in Table 7 is measured via subjective 2012 Afrobarometer respondent perceptions rather than objective administrative records. On the outcome side, DHS electricity availability is assumed to represent grid connection without disaggregating off-grid generators.
confounding: Serious / High concern for causal inference (Some concern for descriptive correlations): Tables 4-5 control for an extensive set of geographic, disease, population-density, petrol, and historical slave-export covariates (plus sensitivity checks excluding Lagos and the Southeast), but static cross-sectional OLS cannot separate post-1976 policy punishment from unobserved historical, cultural, religious, or state-level fiscal confounders correlated with precolonial centralization and >70% Muslim population share. In Table 7, cross-sectional regressions of 2013 service access on 2012 local government perceptions control only for population density, leaving substantial omitted-variable confounding and reverse causality unaddressed.
attrition: Not applicable / Some spatial missingness concern: Individual panel attrition does not apply because the study uses repeated cross-sectional DHS waves rather than a longitudinal cohort; however, two of six geopolitical zones (Northcentral and Southsouth) were not surveyed in 1990, infrastructure items are absent in 1990, and spatial regression coverage drops from 1,415 total LGA-ethnic partitions to 685 available units (N = 631 with complete covariates in Tables 4-5) and N = 127-162 units in the 2012 Afrobarometer regressions (Tables 6-7).
reporting_bias: Some concern: No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported. Several robustness specifications (GCov and GTheil inequality trends, continuous centralization scores, excluding Southeast/Lagos, military president origin interactions, and non-Muslim split-sample tables) are deferred to Supplementary material or noted as 'tables available on request' (Table 4 notes; Note 53), and Note 46 indicates the >70% Muslim threshold was partly informed by exploratory multilevel regressions showing where state-specific centralization slopes turned negative.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak: While the historical narrative identifies specific legal instruments (the 1907 Native Authority Proclamation and the 1976 Local Government Reform Law), legal exposure and statutory compliance are not directly coded or measured. Noncompliance with the 1976 Local Government Reform Law is proxied indirectly by interacting Murdock's c. 1850 centralization dummy with a state-level >70% Muslim indicator from the 1952 census, and services are globally categorized as 'federally administered' (grid electricity, flush toilets) versus 'locally administered' (pit latrines, piped water, boreholes/tubewells) without measuring state-level water statutes, State Water Boards, intergovernmental fiscal transfers, or private household self-provisioning.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate concern: Potable water (piped water, borehole, tubewell, or protected well) and improved sanitation (flush toilet, VIP latrine, or pit latrine with slab) are derived from standardized nationally representative DHS household roster items across 2003-2013. However, these binary indicators capture self-reported availability rather than water safety, supply continuity, or facility functionality; DHS sampling is not stratified for representativeness at the fine 1,415 LGA-ethnic polygon level; and pooling 2003-2013 rounds into static cross-sectional means (labelled 1990-2013 in Tables 1, 4, and 5 despite Note 20 stating infrastructure data exist only for 2003-2013) obscures temporal variation in the regressions.

study_design_identified: Repeated/comparative analytical cross-sectional study using national administrative school census and demographic census microdata (descriptive spatial/tabular analysis and separate binomial logistic regressions for 2011 and 2023)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly adopts a comparative cross-sectional observational design ('um estudo transversal e comparativo referente aos anos de 2011 e 2023') using descriptive cross-tabulations and separate binomial logistic regressions in 2011 and 2023 to estimate school-level and municipal-level determinants of WASH absence. No specific policy or legal intervention is evaluated with a treatment/comparator counterfactual (ruling out ROBINS-I), and schools are not followed as baseline outcome-free cohorts to estimate incidence over time (ruling out JBI Cohort). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
selection_bias: High concern — Although drawn from the nationwide Inep School Census covering 3,424 municipalities, inclusion was conditioned on survival: only rural public elementary schools that remained active and linked to the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023 were retained (PDF p. 3). Because 22,138 rural schools closed or ceased offering regular elementary education over this period, survivor selection bias likely understates historical WASH deprivation among the smallest and most vulnerable closed schools.
measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern — School-level WASH and infrastructure data in the Inep Censo Escolar are self-declared by school principals without systematic external verification ('autodeclarados pelos diretores escolares e não passem por auditoria sistemática', PDF p. 3), with Inep acknowledging major questionnaire errors in other waves (2007-2010, 2017). Additionally, municipal IDHM-income from 2010 was reused for the 2023 cross-section because updated post-2022 IDHM data were unavailable (PDF p. 3), and category 8 ('povos e comunidades tradicionais') existed only in 2023 (PDF p. 5).
confounding: High concern — Multivariable binomial logistic regressions adjust for macroregion, differentiated territorial status, enrollment size, municipal population brackets, rural population percentage and municipal IDHM-income (PDF pp. 5, 8-10), but omit school administrative dependency (state vs. municipal networks) and municipal water/sewerage utility coverage, fail to account for municipal-level clustering, and include endogenous/mutually dependent student yield variables (approval, failure and dropout rates) on the right-hand side as determinants of WASH absence, introducing reverse-causality and collider bias.
attrition: High concern — Between 2011 and 2023, the national universe of rural public elementary schools contracted from 56,544 to 34,406 (a net reduction of 22,138 schools, or 39.2%; PDF p. 3). Restricting the analytic dataset exclusively to schools that remained active and linked to the same municipality in both 2011 and 2023 excludes closed or paralyzed schools without comparing their baseline WASH deprivation against surviving schools.
reporting_bias: High concern — No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and full multivariable logistic regression tables are omitted from the article. The Results section selectively reports prose odds ratios and p-values for highlighted categories (PDF pp. 9-10) without 95% confidence intervals, standard errors, exact regression sample sizes, or model fit/collinearity diagnostics.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (adequate administrative coding of territorial designations; no direct program exposure measurement) — Legal-territorial school categories ('Localização diferenciada': settlement areas, Indigenous lands, quilombola communities, and traditional peoples/communities added in 2023) and rural public elementary school status under Lei nº 9.394/1996 (excluding EJA) are coded directly from official Inep School Census registries (Quadro 1, PDF p. 5). However, federal institutional funding and WASH programs (Funasa Programa Água na Escola, PDDE per-capita funding rules, and PAR) are invoked only narratively in the Introduction and Discussion rather than measured at the school or municipal level (PDF pp. 2, 10-11).
outcome_measurement_quality: High concern — School WASH outcomes are restricted to three crude, unverified self-reported binary indicators in the Censo Escolar: complete absence of water supply, complete absence of sanitation/sewerage, and existence of any toilet (Quadro 1, PDF pp. 5-6). These proxies do not capture drinking-water potability or safety, supply continuity, toilet functionality/privacy, handwashing stations with soap, or menstrual hygiene facilities.

study_design_identified: Comparative historical-institutional four-country case study based on secondary literature and official reports
why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly analyzes the historical-institutional evolution of water and sanitation ownership and regulatory regimes across four country case studies (Britain/England and Wales, Argentina, Côte d'Ivoire, and Israel) using secondary academic/policy literature, agency webpages, and macro statistics. It conducts no primary qualitative fieldwork such as interviews or ethnography (ruling out CASP), applies no systematic review search or screening protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and implements no quantitative quasi-experimental comparator design (ruling out ROBINS-I), making the 13-domain Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the appropriate instrument for a comparative institutional/legal-historical case study.
overall_rating: Weak overall methodological rigor (structured non-validated judgment: strong institutional context and adequate jurisdictional, exposure, and case-selection description, but weak primary legal sourcing, selection neutrality, measurement standardization, causal identification, and confounding control)
selection_bias: High concern — Both the four country cases (chosen specifically because they had already introduced privatization and possessed an extensive published literature) and the secondary sources cited within each case were purposively and non-systematically selected, excluding non-privatizing comparators or poorly documented failures.
measurement_bias: High concern — Neither ownership/regulatory exposures nor water and sanitation performance outcomes are measured with standardized instruments; statistics are compiled uncritically from heterogeneous secondary reports, government webpages, and utility promotional material (such as Aguas Argentinas 2001).
confounding: High concern — No empirical strategy isolates ownership structure from major concurrent historical confounders, including 1980s macroeconomic crises, European Union environmental quality standards in England and Wales, rapid urban demographic growth, hydrological scarcity versus abundance, and multilateral lending conditionality.
attrition: Not applicable / not assessable — The study is a retrospective comparative institutional narrative synthesizing secondary sources rather than a prospective cohort, trial, or panel tracking individual units, though temporal coverage and reported metrics vary unevenly across the four country cases.
reporting_bias: High concern — There is no pre-specified protocol, literature search strategy, or standardized cross-case outcome set; different outcomes and episodes are selectively emphasized in each country narrative depending on available secondary literature.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak — Key legal and institutional milestones (such as England and Wales's 1974 nationalization and 1989 privatization, Buenos Aires's 1993 concession and subsequent renegotiations, Côte d'Ivoire's SODECI lease/concession contracts, and Israel's 1959 Water Law) are described only via secondary academic/World Bank literature and ministry webpages, with zero citations to primary statutes, regulations, or concession texts.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Reported outcomes (network connection counts, coverage percentages, tariff changes, consumer surplus estimates, productivity, and informal vendor price/quality variability) are non-standardized across the four countries and rely on unverified secondary sources and utility self-reports.
where_found: Case selection rationale in Introduction (PDF p. 3 / p. 139); country institutional narratives in Development of Water Supply and Sanitation Sector covering England and Wales, Argentina, Côte d'Ivoire, and Israel (PDF pp. 3-8 / pp. 139-144); cross-case synthesis and GDP per capita comparisons in Discussion and Conclusion (PDF pp. 8-9 / pp. 144-145); source base in References (PDF pp. 10-11 / pp. 146-147). study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal panel observational study (2013-2020 unbalanced panel of 1,157 Brazilian municipality-year observations comparing consortia-participating vs. non-cooperating municipalities using multivariate general linear model regression with state-stratified bootstrapping)
why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the appropriate instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study is a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation of a formal public policy/institutional governance intervention (municipal entry into regional sanitation consortia via programmatic contract vs. a comparator group of stand-alone non-cooperating municipalities) estimating effects on municipal sanitation expenditure and water/wastewater population coverage over 2013-2020.
selection_bias: Serious concern: Inclusion in the 1,157-observation panel required matched non-missing positive water and sewage investment records (log-transformed) from SNIS/FINBRA/IBGE, selecting a small, non-random fraction of municipality-years without defining incident consortium entry vs. prevalent membership or comparing included and excluded municipalities.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Consortium participation, investments, and coverage rely on national administrative/survey databases (IBGE MUNIC, FINBRA, SNIS), but consortium exposure lacks entry/exit timing and contract-type granularity, self-reported municipal accounting/SNIS data vary in accuracy across small vs. large municipalities, and text descriptions mix log-transformed and raw scales.
confounding: Serious concern: Municipalities self-select into regional consortia via city council vote largely due to fiscal distress and low baseline sewage coverage (acknowledged as a driver of cooperation on p. 6), creating reverse causality/confounding by indication; no quasi-experimental design is used, key municipal fiscal/economic confounders are omitted, between-subjects SPSS GLM (11 df) does not absorb municipality fixed effects, and contemporaneous water/sewage investments (post-treatment mediators) are conditioned on.
attrition: Serious concern: Severe missing data across Brazil's ~5,570 municipalities over 2013-2020 reduced the analytic sample to 1,157 observations (1,159 in Table 2), driven by scarce administrative reporting on transaction-cost/investment variables and logarithmic exclusion of zero-investment municipality-years; state-stratified bootstrapping only resampled observed cases without addressing missing-data bias.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol was registered, and multiple internal reporting inconsistencies appear (Table 1 has no content; sample size is 1,159 in Table 2 vs. 1,157 in Table 3; Density is omitted from Table 4 without explanation due to exact log-collinearity with Population and Area; Section 5 claims service coverage improved under cooperative agreements despite negative/lower sewage coverage estimates for cooperation in Section 4 and Tables 3-4).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak: Although Section 2.3 describes Brazil's constitutional decentralization, 2007 federal sanitation guidelines, programmatic contracts, city council voting rules, and 2020 Sanitation Legal Framework Act, the empirical model collapses institutional participation into a binary consortium dummy (1/0) and proxies contract management complexity only by water-only vs. combined water-and-wastewater scope, while Table 1 (contractual tools) is blank in the published PDF.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Outcomes (municipal total sanitation expenditure and indices of total population served by water and sewage services) derive from standardized official national sources (FINBRA, IBGE, SNIS), but measure only aggregate spending and nominal population coverage without service continuity, water quality, or actual wastewater treatment performance, and Section 4 inconsistently reports log and unlogged group means.

study_design_identified: Single-district public-administration teaching case / institutional implementation case study (descriptive narrative case history citing secondary administrative and third-party validation statistics and one informant quote, with no research Methods section or comparator arm)
why_tool_chosen: S926 is a single-district institutional/public-administration case history of sanitation governance and statutory scheme convergence in Nadia District, India, published as an educational case study in Emerald Emerging Markets Case Studies. ROBINS-I does not apply because it is a single-case history with no comparator arm. CASP Qualitative Checklist is ill-suited because the paper contains no research aims, qualitative sampling, interview protocol, ethical statement, or qualitative data analysis—instead ending with pedagogical discussion questions for management students. Unlike pure mathematical simulations or non-empirical commentaries (NONE), the paper documents a concrete single-jurisdiction institutional implementation episode citing baseline and validation metrics, making the 13-domain Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the most appropriate instrument to transparently evaluate both its rich institutional context and its severe empirical/methodological limitations.
overall_rating: High methodological concern / Weak empirical rigor (structured non-validated judgment: 2 strong, 1 adequate, 9 weak, 1 not assessable across 13 domains)
selection_bias: High concern / Weak: Purposive single-case selection of Nadia District after it won the 2015 UN Public Services Award and was declared India's first ODF district; narrative relies on illustrative examples and a single quoted protagonist (District Magistrate P.B. Salim) with no informant sampling criteria and no reported sampling methodology for cited surveys.
measurement_bias: High concern / Weak: Baseline open defecation and post-campaign toilet coverage (60% to 97%) and usage (57% to 99.8%) are cited from secondary administrative and UNICEF/partner reports without operational definitions or survey instruments in the text (and Exhibits 3, 5, and 6 on PDF pp. 14-16 are non-extracted figure graphics); signed household ODF declarations and neighborhood volunteer monitoring of 'violators'/'defaulters' create strong social desirability and administrative reporting biases, while child health improvements are asserted without clinical metrics.
confounding: High concern / Weak: Single-district before-after narrative (Nadia District, 2013-2015) with no comparison district, no statistical adjustment, and no separation of project leadership effects from concurrent national/state sanitation funding, demographic/economic differences across blocks, or bundled multi-agency co-interventions.
attrition: Not assessable / No information: No longitudinal participant cohort is tracked by the authors, and sample attrition, non-response, or missing data in the cited 2013 baseline survey and 2015 third-party validation surveys are not reported.
reporting_bias: High concern / Weak: Published as an educational management teaching case with no research protocol and an explicit disclaimer that names, financial, and recognizable details may be disguised; selectively emphasizes award-winning successes without systematic reporting of coercion complaints, construction quality failures, post-2015 usage slippage, or block-level heterogeneity.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Richly describes administrative hierarchies and institutional convergence across statutory/national schemes (MGNREGA, NRLM, NBA, SSA, ICDS), Gram Panchayats, and village Para Najardari monitoring committees, but cites zero statutory provisions, rules, formal government orders, or budgetary circulars, and carries a teaching-case confidentiality disclaimer.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Relies on secondary summary figures (0.35 million toilets constructed, >336,000 families reached, 97% coverage, 99.8% usage among ages 4+) whose underlying survey protocols and Exhibit 5-6 graphics are absent from the text, alongside unquantified claims of reduced sanitation-related child disease.

study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental non-randomized policy evaluation using a cross-sectional modified difference-in-differences design (exploiting spatial variation in phased-in village rollout of Peru's PETT land-titling program interacted with pre-program household title status, supplemented by difference-in-differences with propensity score matching) on a 2004 rural household survey (N = 3,204; analytic N = 3,182).
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates the causal effect of a non-randomized government land-titling intervention (PETT) with explicit comparator groups (program vs. non-program villages interacted with prior-titled vs. previously untitled households) using a quasi-experimental modified difference-in-differences estimator and propensity score matching. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the required appraisal tool for non-randomized quasi-experimental policy evaluations (DiD, PSM).
selection_bias: Moderate risk — The 2004 Land Titling Special Project Survey sampled 3,204 rural households stratified by region (coast, highlands, jungle) to represent PETT program and non-program areas (p. 5), but data collection occurred 4–11 years after PETT rollout began, creating potential post-intervention selection via land sales or out-migration, and primary sampling frame details and response rates are not reported in this paper.
measurement_bias: Moderate risk — Both prior-title classification and all water, sanitation, electricity, 5-year connection, and expenditure outcomes are measured via retrospective household self-reports in the 2004 survey without administrative registry verification, utility billing records, or physical inspection of water source protection and quality.
confounding: Serious risk — Identification relies on a cross-sectional modified difference-in-differences interaction (village PETT arrival x no prior title) using a single 2004 post-rollout survey without pre-intervention waves to test parallel trends (p. 8; Note 14, p. 12); village rollout timing may be endogenous (p. 4); village-level baseline wealth and infrastructure capacity are unobserved beyond coarse 3-region fixed effects; and regression covariates include post-treatment 2004 household characteristics (workers, home business ownership, rental income) that may be affected by titling.
attrition: Low risk — As a single-wave cross-sectional survey there is no longitudinal panel attrition, and item missingness in the regression analyses is minimal (3,182 of 3,204 surveyed households analyzed; 0.7% missing), although initial survey response rates and item missingness on connection-year dates are not reported.
reporting_bias: Moderate risk — No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol exists, and secondary analyses—including the difference-in-differences propensity-score-matching estimates (p. 9) and monthly water payment regressions (p. 11)—are summarized verbally without reporting point estimates or standard errors.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate — The paper situates PETT in its statutory context (Legislative Decree 25902 of 1991 and 1996 extension to all rural estates, p. 4) and distinguishes village-level PETT rollout from household PETT title, other title, and no-title status, but reconstructs pre-PETT title status ('no prior title') retrospectively from 2004 self-reports under the assumption that 'other titles' were held prior to PETT rather than linking to cadastre/registry records (Note 19, p. 12).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Survey items disaggregate specific water supply modes (indoor tap, outdoor tap, fountain, artisan well/spring, river, tanker truck/vendor), sanitation/septic access, recent network connections, and financing sources (Tables 3 and 6), but rely exclusively on self-report and code all fountains and artisan wells/springs as 'improved water sources' without verifying physical protection, water quality, <1 km distance, or >=20 L/day quantity thresholds noted in Note 16.
